factions.history:
The established Dominion
The Verminhorde Dominion replaces the Ratkin Clans completely. Its authoritative faction reference remains the user-provided Codex Verminhorde Dominion Definitive 11th Edition v1.1. This expansion does not rename Verminia, replace Varkrul or manufacture a contradictory founding myth. The original source describes a subterranean empire of mass infantry, artillery, scavenged armour, tunnel warfare and intelligence theft, held together by brood production and competing authorities.

Verminia the All-Mother stands above the Thirteen Daughters, Great Clans, military commanders and technical institutions. Varkrul’s warfare targets the systems that keep an enemy functional rather than merely its strongest warrior. The Dread-Confessors and Feast of Memory turn death into intelligence, while the Scrap-Seers recombine captured technologies. These source-derived features remain the standard against which the new factions have been differentiated.

Strength and its cost
The source makes the Dominion powerful but constrained. Accelerated population replacement consumes biomass; hybrid technology is hard to maintain; tunnels can be flooded or collapsed; clan competition wastes resources; memory rites carry contamination risks. These costs matter because an army with infinite replacements, perfect stolen technology and unanswerable tunnels would offer little strategic interaction.

The current game represents only part of this depth: Pressure, Broken enemies, artillery, sabotage, memory harvest, engineering repair, tunnel travel and a limited Chitterhold replacement. The tactical spell powers assigned to Confessors are explicitly original Ashcrown adaptations, not claims about the source datasheet. The detailed page mapping and omissions remain in CODEX-MAPPING.md.

The Dominion in the Ashcrown setting
Relations with the twelve other powers are new setting material. The Dominion competes with the Kharad for deep infrastructure, with the Cinderjaw for salvage and with the Continuum and Vesperglass over the value and ownership of memory. It threatens the Compact by entering beneath civic systems and the Synod by altering water and soil unseen. Sauridian archives and Lumen predictive instruments are especially attractive technical prizes.

Neither holy nor corrupted sisterhood is merely another source of expendable infantry. The Dawn’s credibility can interrupt the dependency networks on which hidden warrens rely; the Hollow Star’s soul claims conflict with the Dominion’s practical treatment of all life as resource. These tensions create new campaign premises without retroactively placing the original codex’s external-setting wars inside Ashcrown’s chronology.

Skarrath Deep
Source pp.9 and 66: the throne-warren capital and seat of the All-Mother.

Gnawspire
Source p.9: a forge world devoted to dismantling and rebuilding captured technology.

Mirehollow
Source p.9: a Rotlung laboratory world of chemical trials and hidden infrastructure.

Thundermaw
Source p.35: artillery foundries and siege schools. In-game doctrine increases suppression from artillery hits.

Deepdelve
Source p.39: tunnel infrastructure and reserve assaults. In-game doctrine expands tunnel eligibility and reduces travel AP cost.

Chitterhold
Source p.42: replacement warfare. In-game doctrine returns one lost Clawrat formation at half strength for Biomass.

The remaining Great Clans
All thirteen remain part of the supplied lore. Ten clan packages and most of their tactical orders are not yet mechanically implemented; their existence is not replaced by the three available doctrines.

Verminia the All-Mother
Source pp.14–15 and 89: the sovereign and biological centre of the Dominion. The Quiet Dread adds a playable colossal manifestation and renewable brood mechanic as an original adaptation.

Varkrul Thirteenclaw
Source pp.26–28 and 89. The established warlord whose Breaking Number doctrine attacks enemy systems. His full character profile is not implemented in the current battle roster.

Seraphyx Thirteen-Veil
Source p.111 supersedes p.90. The Watching Daughter is playable using an adapted Watcher’s Dossier and venom needler. Her game-role commander eligibility and sabotage are original adaptations.

Source chronology
The codex’s Ashen Reach, Red Birthing, Mirehollow and Lathros campaigns remain in its original chronology. They are not silently relabelled as Ash Calendar events.

New premise — The Stolen Meridian
A Dominion retrieval force discovers that a Sauridian reactor is part of a wider living maintenance network. The operation becomes a choice between taking a component and awakening the system around it.

New premise — The Memory Siege
Vesperglass, Continuum and Dominion forces contest a damaged archive containing incompatible records of the same battle. Each side wants a different kind of victory from the same evidence.

factions.history:
The alliance that refused a crown
The Aurelian Compact began as the emergency government of seven human cities whose orbital supply network failed during the Crown fracture. Each possessed one indispensable resource: food, water, reactors, archives, shipyards, medicines or rail. None could survive the others’ destruction. Their first treaty was written on ammunition crates during a winter siege, and its most enduring clause forbade any city from monopolising the maintenance knowledge needed to keep another alive.

Over three centuries the seven-city pact became a federation of inhabited worlds, station republics and frontier duchies. It inherited the uniforms and cavalry traditions of several dead empires without accepting a single imperial bloodline. Its citizens disagree about almost everything except the memory of what isolation costs. Aurelian rhetoric celebrates the ordinary person carrying a public duty through extraordinary danger. Its darker reality is that wealthy cities can disguise their priorities as everyone’s emergency.

Citizenship and command
The Assembly of Lamps apportions votes between population and essential contributions. An elected First Marshal receives operational control only for a declared emergency; renewal requires civilian assent. Provincial generals retain considerable freedom, creating a military that is adaptable but sometimes painfully slow to coordinate. The Civil Audit accompanies armies to investigate requisition, prisoner treatment and the temptation to extend an emergency indefinitely.

Service is an occupation rather than a hereditary caste. Soldiers return to trades, teach reservists and carry veterans’ voting rights back into local politics. Cavalry houses retain ceremonial titles but cannot exclude recruits by birth. Aether colleges are publicly chartered. Their arguments with intelligence officers over secrecy are constant, because a spell that powers a hospital can often be adapted into a weapon. The Compact’s greatest internal conflict is whether protection justifies temporary dictatorship, and how long temporary can honestly last.

An army of connected arms
Lantern Fusiliers establish a reliable firing line while Wardens occupy dangerous ground. Hussars scout, screen and pursue; Cuirassier Exolancers wait for a decisive heavy charge. Railcrawlers engage enemy armour and Sunfall batteries dislodge entrenched formations. Cantors provide magical support without replacing the army’s logistical base. Engineers and railway troops are considered combat essentials, not background labour.

Interlocking Fire represents their common target language: a first volley identifies range and movement, allowing the next unit to shoot more accurately. The doctrine fails when officers cluster too closely or stop listening to reconnaissance. A Compact force should win by choosing where to combine ordinary tools. It should not possess the strongest version of every specialist weapon. Its common equipment simplifies repair, but its coalition supply schedules and dependence on roads create vulnerabilities a patient enemy can exploit.

The frontier bargain
The Compact buys pressure machinery from the Kharad and grain from worlds protected by the Verdant Synod. Both relationships are uneasy. Industrial expansion sometimes destroys the very ecosystems needed to feed the cities, while a dwarf contract can bind a future government to a predecessor’s expensive promise. The Daughters are trusted as impartial rescuers but resist being treated as an auxiliary military branch.

The Dominion is feared because it can make a supposedly secure city dependent on hostile infrastructure without moving a visible border. The Compact therefore maintains independent water maps and rotating ammunition depots. Vesperglass agents exploit electoral scandals; the Hollow Star targets the exhausted citizens who believe public institutions have abandoned them. The Compact’s answer must be competent government as well as victory. A defended city that no longer trusts its defenders has already lost a different war.

Aurel Gate
The assembly capital occupies a rebuilt orbital elevator. Its public archive contains the original seven-city treaty and every subsequent emergency renewal.

Vesper Plain
A grain world of railway towns and cavalry schools. It is unrelated to the Vesperglass Cabals; the shared root comes from an older word for evening.

Kestrel Foundry
Shipyards and steelworks circle a cold moon. Its unions supply both artillery crews and some of the Assembly’s most persistent critics.

The Seven Lamps
The constitutional centre prizes combined-arms professionalism. Its officers fear the fragmentation of the alliance more than any single invading army.

The Marcher Leagues
Frontier worlds favour scouts, light cavalry and local initiative. They resent delayed reinforcements and are vulnerable to charismatic would-be protectors.

The Cuirassier Compact
Heavy cavalry houses converted inherited privileges into public service charters. Their rivalry concerns honour, funding and whose casualties politicians remember.

The Civic Arsenal
Engineers, railway officers and gun schools argue that a well-supplied infantry company is worth more than a spectacular hero. They are frequently right and rarely popular.

First Marshal Cassian Rook
Rook rose after refusing an order to destroy a city’s water plant to deny it to the enemy. His subsequent defence saved the plant and cost his regiment half its strength. He now chairs an alliance that admires his restraint while demanding cheaper victories. His command style coordinates fire, reserves and withdrawals; his private fear is becoming indispensable enough that the Assembly stops questioning him.

General Maerin Holt
Holt was a railway surveyor before a raid stranded her work crews behind enemy lines. She organised an evacuation along an abandoned freight spur and later rebuilt it into an offensive supply route. Her campaigns turn on bridges, fuel and repair workshops. Rivals call her unimaginative until their brilliant advance runs out of ammunition beside a depot she built weeks earlier.

Warden-General Selka Marr
Marr led the campaign to publish safe Aether practices after a military laboratory accident poisoned a civilian district. She is both an accomplished Cantor and a stubborn constitutionalist. On campaign she uses wards and precision magic to keep ordinary troops functional. She distrusts prophecy that cannot be cross-examined and has repeatedly challenged Lumen seers to disclose the alternatives they chose not to mention.

18 AC — The Winter of Seven Lamps
The founding cities pooled supplies during a siege and rejected the admiral who offered protection in exchange for hereditary rule. The treaty became the Compact’s foundation.

204 AC — The Iron Road War
Holt’s predecessors defeated a much larger raiding host by protecting junctions rather than every mile of rail. Modern mobile reserve doctrine dates from this campaign.

309 AC — The Buried Referendum
A city voted to leave the Compact just as Dominion tunnels appeared below its reservoirs. Rook protected its evacuation despite the vote, establishing that citizenship rights were not payment for political loyalty.

factions.history:
Civilisation under pressure
The Kharad Vault Concord was born in sealed dwarf habitats where the difference between politics and engineering was often a door that would not close. Their bodies adapted to high gravity and restricted environments, but their culture was shaped more profoundly by interdependence. Air had to be accounted for; structural warnings had to be believed; an expert could not safely be silenced because a powerful family disliked the calculation.

Before the fracture, the Vaults maintained deep Crown foundations for rulers who rarely visited them. When those rulers disappeared, the dwarfs inherited debts, dangerous machinery and millions of people trapped behind failing seals. The Concord joined independent holds through a common emergency code. Its founding oath does not demand that a hold never fall. It demands that those who know it is failing tell the truth while evacuation is still possible.

The government of recorded promises
Each hold elects a Castellan and a civic pressure council. Guilds certify competence, but certification can be challenged before travelling rune judges. The Nine Seals govern air, water, heat, labour, defence, inheritance, asylum, debt and emergency command. A promise is recorded with its conditions and witnesses so that later rulers cannot conveniently remember only the flattering parts.

This system preserves institutional memory and produces formidable bureaucracy. Old contracts sometimes outlive the circumstances that made them reasonable. Reformers argue that the purpose of an oath is protection, while traditionalists fear that reinterpretation turns every obligation into a suggestion. Families adopt apprentices across bloodlines, and a master’s reputation includes the independence of those apprentices. The most shameful guild failure is not making a mistake; it is concealing one until someone else dies from it.

The slow wall of iron
Kharad infantry carry heavy plate, precise mass-drivers and portable seal shields. There is no conventional cavalry arm. Short-ranged boreframes and walking bastions provide the counterattack that mounted troops supply elsewhere. Artillery uses gravity manipulation to punish fixed positions, and rune surveyors reinforce the geometry of a defended line. A planned withdrawal is drilled as carefully as an advance because the Concord has buried enough brave fools behind doors they refused to abandon.

Anchored Plate makes stationary infantry particularly difficult to shift. Movement exposes joints and disrupts overlapping shield patterns, so the army must decide when ground is worth leaving. It suffers on widely separated objectives and against opponents who refuse a decisive engagement. Heavy ammunition, replacement seals and specialist maintenance are expensive. An invulnerable-looking line can become helpless if its transports are cut off or its commanders defend a strategically irrelevant fortress out of pride.

Memory without petrification
The Vaults trade with the Compact and Sauridian Dynasty, argue with the Synod over mineral extraction and compete bitterly with Dominion tunnellers. They distinguish a legal salvage claim from theft even when the stolen machine is already a wreck. Cinderjaw engineers earn grudging admiration for practical invention; Freehold warbosses earn less admiration when they treat an invoice as a challenge to single combat.

The Sepulchral Continuum unsettles Kharad law because it asks whether a dead signatory can still amend a contract. Rune judges are divided. The Lumen Principalities are considered unreliable negotiators when they invoke futures that witnesses cannot examine. The Concord’s long-term danger is becoming a perfect archive of obligations that no living society can fulfil. Its best generals defend the people who make promises, not merely the inscriptions left behind.

Kharad Nhal
A high-gravity world honeycombed with civic vaults. Its largest assembly hall is built beside a deliberately exposed pressure gauge.

The Nine-Seal Ring
An orbital habitat chain housing neutral courts, arbitration foundries and refugee docks. Weapons are checked alongside commercial accounts.

Flintwake Deeps
A contested mining frontier whose ores can stabilise Aether reactors. Its seismic maps are among the most frequently stolen documents in the setting.

Holds of the First Seal
Traditional defensive armies favour Hearthguard and prepared gun lines. Their strength is discipline; their weakness is treating inherited boundaries as sacred strategy.

The Open Ledger
Reformist guilds prioritise mobile repair, evacuation planning and transparent command. Their opponents accuse them of turning every oath into a committee discussion.

Deepmeasure Circuits
Rune judges and gravitic engineers unite science with binding magic. They refuse to certify a weapon whose failure modes its sponsors will not disclose.

The Unhoused Companies
Dwarfs whose holds were destroyed serve as expeditionary troops. They are determined to earn new homes without repeating the mistakes that cost the old ones.

High Castellan Dorrik Vane
Dorrik ordered the evacuation of his ancestral hold six hours before its central shield failed. He saved its population and lost a family tomb containing nine centuries of records. Traditionalists call him the Castellan Who Left; survivors elected him Keeper of the Nine Seals. He commands slowly because he wants every officer to understand the withdrawal plan before anyone fires.

Maela Flintledger
Maela proved that an ammunition guild had altered maintenance records to conceal a lethal defect. Her testimony destroyed a powerful patron and made her an unlikely military hero. She commands engineers with unusual autonomy and can hold an army together after its armour should have failed. Her ambition is a Concord where admitting uncertainty is recognised as professional strength.

Orrun Deepmeasure
Orrun is a rune judge who served inside the failing Crown foundations during a century-long maintenance mission. He trusts measurements, but has learned that a frightened commander can distort their interpretation without falsifying a number. His battlefield magic stabilises forces at critical moments. He is investigating whether some of the Crown’s oldest failure warnings were deliberately ignored.

7 AC — The Closing of the Nine Seals
Independent holds adopted common emergency law after a rescue mission failed because three incompatible authorities each claimed final command.

221 AC — The Airless Siege
Kharad troops defeated an invading fleet by evacuating outer habitats and fighting from sealed internal fortresses. The victory created their modern layered defence doctrine.

300 AC — The Flintledger Hearings
Public exposure of fraudulent shell casings nearly split the Concord. Maela’s reforms survived because front-line companies refused to load unverified ammunition.

factions.history:
The people who survived tomorrow
The Lumen Arc Principalities descend from elven observatory fleets that studied the Crown before its fracture. Their navigators learned to perceive branching probabilities through resonant crystal. They could not see one fixed future, but could compare many incomplete ones. This gave them a reputation for impossible foresight and encouraged a disastrous belief that superior information justified superior authority.

During the fracture, the fleets saved millions by abandoning routes they knew would collapse. They also abandoned people they might have saved in less probable futures. The argument over those choices became the defining wound of modern elven politics. The Principalities now insist that prediction must be witnessed, debated and limited. Their exiled rivals, the Vesperglass Cabals, maintain that any limit on foresight is cowardice. Both remember the same catastrophe, but they preserve different lists of its victims.

Houses, intervals and dissent
A Principality is a network of star-habitats and planetary enclaves led by a house entrusted with maintaining a particular navigational or civic function. Leadership combines hereditary continuity with formal challenge: a successor must defend decisions before citizens who may have lived long enough to remember the predecessor’s original promises. Seers advise councils but cannot legally rule by prophecy alone.

The Interval Courts examine whether a prediction was manipulated through selective disclosure. Their proceedings are slow and imperfect. Wealthy houses can afford better instruments, making unequal access to foresight a persistent political problem. Elven longevity encourages patience, but also allows grievances to survive long after their practical causes disappear. Younger citizens increasingly demand the right to choose an uncertain life instead of being protected into a destiny calculated before their birth.

War in the space between choices
Lumen armies are small, expensive and highly trained. Prism Linekeepers deliver accurate fire, Dawnthread Blades strike where a defence is momentarily disordered, and Arcwind Cavaliers exploit rapidly changing angles. Their grav engines favour speed over heavy plating. Seers and lattice artisans are essential specialists whose loss cannot be replaced by a larger supply of ordinary recruits.

Foresight supplies a native reroll to missed firearm attacks, while Swift movement preserves their advantage in positioning. These are constrained expressions of prediction, not invulnerability. They remain vulnerable to saturation, disruption and opponents willing to accept losses the Lumen models consider irrational. Thin armour and low formation strength punish mistakes. Their greatest tactical danger is believing an elegant plan must be correct because it was expensive to calculate.

The obligation to remain surprised
The Principalities maintain uneasy scholarly exchanges with the Sauridians and respectful arguments with the Daughters about whether a good result can justify withholding the truth. The Compact values their navigation services but distrusts unequal treaties based on secret predictions. The Vault Concord demands written contingencies for every promised future. The Synod refuses to let its forests be reduced to variables in an elven model.

War with Vesperglass is intimate and vicious because each side knows the other’s methods. The Principalities also fear Verminhorde memory theft: a captured seer could reveal not just a plan, but the discarded alternatives surrounding it. Their most controversial reform requires commanders to preserve records of failed predictions. A civilisation that deletes its mistakes from the archive can become certain of its own wisdom just as it becomes incapable of learning.

Auralis Span
A chain of transparent habitats orbiting a dim star. Public observatories allow citizens to inspect the instruments that inform state policy.

The Quiet Meridian
A neutral navigation station where hostile houses exchange emergency route data. Violence here is treated as an attack on every ship still travelling.

Ilyr’s Last Garden
A planetary refuge containing plants rescued from worlds the fleets could not save. Each grove bears a plaque describing the abandoned alternatives.

House Vaer
Reformers favour citizen line troops and open predictive archives. Their enemies accuse them of sacrificing decisive advantage to procedural conscience.

House Quill
Fleet aristocrats specialise in grav cavalry and rapid intervention. They are often first to a crisis and impatient with councils that have not yet agreed it exists.

The Last Interval
Seers advocate strict limits on temporal expenditure. They believe repeated manipulation can destroy futures that have not yet acquired anyone capable of defending them.

The Unwritten League
Younger citizens reject hereditary prediction and prefer scouts, empirical intelligence and plans that admit uncertainty. Some accuse them of throwing away their people’s greatest gift.

Strategarch Aelith Vaer
Aelith published the probability tables behind a celebrated victory and revealed that a neighbouring colony had been quietly written off. Her house nearly expelled her before the colony’s survivors made her their protector. She commands through shared situational awareness, expecting subordinates to challenge predictions. Her political project is a Principality whose citizens can knowingly refuse the future their rulers recommend.

Ilyr Sen of the Last Interval
Ilyr remembers several histories that never became real. This makes him wise about consequences and unreliable about ordinary chronology. He once prevented a civil war by destroying the instrument that proved he would win it. He now hunts evidence that too much predictive intervention is narrowing the entire species’ future into a small set of increasingly violent possibilities.

Admiral Thessa Quill
Thessa built her reputation by taking a relief fleet through a route every model rated unacceptable. She saved the target habitat and lost the flagship carrying her family. Neither fact cancels the other in her mind. Her cavalry doctrine creates several simultaneous dilemmas, forcing opponents to make choices too quickly for even a seer to calculate comfortably.

3 AC — The Choosing of Routes
Observatory fleets escaped the fracture through selected corridors. Their rescue decisions created the moral and political division that later split the elven people.

96 AC — The Trial of Unseen Lives
The first Interval Court convicted a prince for hiding an unfavourable prediction from an ally. The ruling established that prophecy did not erase responsibility.

310 AC — The Battle of Three Tomorrows
Lumen and Vesperglass fleets each predicted the other’s victory. Thessa forced an unmodelled evacuation, saving civilians while both military plans collapsed.

The Hollow Star is a tempting customer and a dangerous competitor. Cabals sell memories; the Convent claims ownership of the soul that remembers. The Continuum treats involuntary memory extraction as an assault on civic personhood, making their wars unusually ideological. The Daughters maintain shelters where escaped debtors are allowed to give testimony without selling it. Cabal propaganda calls those shelters theft. Their rulers fear them precisely because that claim sounds less convincing when spoken aloud.

Vesperglass
A duskward habitat ring with mirrored courts above heavily shielded vaults. Its public plazas are designed so everyone can be watched from somewhere beautiful.

The Silent Exchange
A mobile market whose location is communicated through encrypted fragments of song. Buyers may conceal their faces but must declare what they are willing to lose.

Nacre Hollow
A captured moon used to grow neural crystal. Its workers preserve a clandestine archive of everything the official vault says never happened.

The Crownless Vault
Nysera’s oldest cabal specialises in political leverage and precision troops. It claims neutrality while ensuring every negotiated peace leaves someone in its debt.

The Quiet Debt
Assassin syndicates prefer a few irreversible acts to prolonged warfare. Their internal honour concerns exact contracts, not the innocence of the target.

The Unlived Bank
Oracle houses trade predictive possibilities and finance other cabals’ campaigns. Their accounts include obligations that will mature only if a particular future occurs.

The Broken Mirror
Insurgent retainers seek to abolish hereditary memory debt. They still use raiding tactics, and freedom from the cabals does not automatically make them merciful conquerors.

Archoness Nysera Vhal
Nysera’s birth name disappeared during a vault fire that killed all seven people entitled to inherit ahead of her. She neither confirms nor denies responsibility. Her long reign depends on balancing clients who each believe they possess a secret capable of removing her. On the battlefield she coordinates accurate fire and exploits wounded enemies; politically she prefers debts that can be collected repeatedly to victories that end a relationship.

Vael Corven, the Quiet Debt
Vael once discovered that the memory of his childhood had been assembled from several unrelated debtors. He now collects proof against the cabal that made him, while remaining one of its most profitable commanders. His raids target evidence stores and command structures. He is dangerous because he genuinely wants freedom and has never accepted that other people might deserve it without first becoming useful to him.

Seer-Matron Eshara Vey
Eshara lends unrealised futures to clients facing impossible choices. The interest is paid in possibilities their descendants will never receive. She sees herself as a practical banker in a universe of scarcity, and dislikes crude cruelty because it damages collateral. Her magical support makes small forces extraordinarily efficient, but every apparent rescue creates an obligation she intends to enforce.

41 AC — The Exile of the Mirror Houses
A dispute over evacuation archives became armed secession. The departing houses took navigation instruments and the memories of thousands who had not consented to leave.

188 AC — The War Without Birthdays
A cabal attempted to erase a rival’s lineage from every vault. Surviving families now celebrate the day their identities were recovered rather than the dates of their births.

307 AC — The Shelter of Unpaid Names
Dawn sisters defended a refugee station containing escaped memory debtors. The cabals lost the battle and an expensive propaganda campaign insisting the refugees were stolen property.

factions.history:
A republic after death
The Sepulchral Continuum formed when a failing colony discovered that its ancestor archive could inhabit artificial bodies through Aether resonance. The first revenants were not conquerors or aristocrats. They were engineers needed to repair systems no living person fully understood. Their return saved the colony and immediately created a constitutional crisis: did the dead possess authority, employment rights, family claims and a duty to leave when their work was finished?

The Continuance Charter answered with a principle still contested today. Identity may survive death, but consent must survive with it. A citizen can authorise a limited second service, decline resurrection, or demand final release. Enemies often see only skeleton troops and assume a mindless necromantic tyranny. Some Continuum officials encourage that fear. Others spend their entire second lives proving that a dead society need not become a society ruled forever by the dead.

The living register
The government divides authority between living citizens, returned citizens and independent Notaries who verify identity and consent. Neither population can amend the Charter alone. A restored person must demonstrate continuity through private memories and chosen witnesses; imperfect reconstruction is treated as a new person with rights, not a defective copy to be discarded.

Bodies range from carefully preserved remains to ceramic ossuary frames and spectral projections supported by machines. Wealth still distorts access to desirable forms. Poor citizens may return in standard military chassis while the rich commission graceful replicas. Reformers seek equal restoration rights, but a universal promise would exceed the archive’s capacity. Families must negotiate grief rather than have it erased. A returned parent may be legally the same person while having missed decades that cannot be repaired by a new body.

The army that keeps its appointments
Testament Cohorts and Sarcophagus Guard absorb losses that would exhaust ordinary troops. Dreadwake Knights provide mounted counterattacks; artillery carries destructive resonance in shells patterned after funerary bells. Notaries restore damaged formations by reconnecting their bodies to intact identity records. Suppression cannot reduce their action allowance, although disrupted senses can still impair accuracy.

Continuance is maintenance, not limitless regeneration. The game restores small amounts of health only to surviving infantry near a caster; destroyed formations do not simply stand up again. In the lore, a body can be rebuilt only if its archive and consent record remain intact. Severing local necromantic links, isolating Notaries or destroying storage infrastructure can make losses permanent. The army is also relatively slow, and its conservative command culture sometimes mistakes endurance for an answer to manoeuvre.

The right to an ending
The Continuum trades legal expertise and ancient technical knowledge with the Compact and Kharad. Both appreciate its reliability while fearing contracts that might never expire. Its relations with the Synod are complicated: some groves welcome the respectful preservation of memory, while others see revenant bodies as life withheld from natural cycles.

Vesperglass memory slavery and Hollow Star soul consumption are fundamental enemies of the Charter. Against them the Continuum fights to protect personhood rather than merely territory. Verminhorde memory harvesting is regarded as theft from the unconsenting dead, though Dominion officials argue that discarded neural traces cannot own anything. The Continuum’s own danger is quieter: officials can indefinitely postpone release by declaring another emergency. Its integrity depends on remaining willing to honour the final wish of citizens whose continued service would be very useful.

Morrowrest
The founding colony surrounds a vast public archive. Gardens above the storage vaults are maintained jointly by living and returned families.

The Quiet Parliament
A station whose chambers alternate between warm living quarters and resonance halls. Every session ends by reading the names of citizens granted final release.

Ossuary Reach
A frontier of industrial tomb-cities repeatedly attacked for their rare memory substrates. Its defence forces contain many of the Continuum’s oldest volunteers.

The Testament Legions
Charter loyalists emphasise controlled restoration and disciplined line warfare. They refuse to deploy a citizen whose service consent cannot be verified.

The Eternal Custodians
Traditionalists believe survival requires longer terms of posthumous service. Their critics fear that emergency duty is becoming ownership.

The Last Door
Notaries dedicated to release rights specialise in destroying hostile soul machinery. They are prepared to dismantle their own state if it becomes a prison.

The Unremembered
New persons formed from incomplete archives seek recognition independent of the dead they resemble. Their innovative methods challenge the assumption that age creates authority.

First Executor Nemea Sorn
Nemea wrote the legal ruling that prevented a restored governor from reclaiming office automatically. She later died defending the archive containing that ruling and returned for a limited military term. Her authority rests on disciplined adherence to limits she could easily evade. She has published the date on which she intends to leave command permanently, forcing her government to prepare for a future without her.

Grave-Marshal Othric Vale
Othric has led cavalry through four reconstructed bodies, each with subtly different instincts. He keeps the old armour beside his quarters to remember that continuity requires work. His doctrine uses endurance to hold an enemy in place before a decisive mounted strike. He fears losing his capacity to grieve more than losing another body.

High Notary Iseth Marr
Iseth is alive and has explicitly declined future restoration. That choice makes her a trusted guardian of the release process and a target for those who think continuity should be compulsory. She maintains emergency keys capable of shutting down compromised archive networks. In battle she restores troops carefully, refusing shortcuts that might return someone different merely because the army needs another rifle.

22 AC — The First Return
Dead engineers restored a failing colony’s thermal systems. The resulting argument over their rights produced the earliest Continuance Charter.

139 AC — The Succession of Empty Chairs
Returned governors attempted to resume office across six worlds. Nemea’s ruling and a short civil war established that memory of power did not confer current authority.

311 AC — The Last Door Campaign
Notaries destroyed a Hollow Star soul refinery and released its prisoners rather than recruit them. The military cost was high; the precedent was deliberately absolute.

factions.history:
The nations that would not be fenced
The Hornbound Exodus is a confederation of beastfolk populations displaced by the Crown’s industrial expansion and later by its collapse. Goatfolk, centaurs, minotaurs and many smaller lineages were classified by former empires as labour categories before they were recognised as peoples. Some inhabited worlds for millennia; others were shaped by ancient gene-work whose records survive only as property inventories. The Exodus refuses to make that distinction a test of legitimacy.

Its founding migration began when several communities discovered that their supposedly temporary resettlement camps had become hereditary estates. They broke the perimeter fences, seized transport and carried their schools, elders and seed stocks into the open country. The road became a political institution: no person should lose their right to leave merely because a government finds their labour convenient. This ideal makes the Exodus a refuge, but also creates difficulty whenever a common decision requires a community to stay and fight.

Hearths on the move
A caravan nation consists of hearth councils connected by route assemblies. A Road-Mother or Road-Father coordinates a migration season but does not own the herds, wagons or people travelling with it. Large communities include fixed farms and towns whose residents maintain membership through trade and the preservation of safe passage. Mobility is a right, not a command that everyone must remain nomadic.

Centaur populations often serve as dragoons and couriers, while minotaur work-clans specialise in heavy construction and assault. These are practical traditions rather than moral ranks. Storykeepers record roads as relationships: where water was freely shared, where a bridge was defended, where a host betrayed guests. The biggest internal divide lies between communities seeking recognised borders and those who believe borders inevitably become cages. Both can point to real histories that support their fear.

Raiding as a means of survival
Hornbound armies move rapidly, strike logistics and avoid prolonged artillery duels. Rifle herds screen centaur dragoons; Stormcart Chariots provide mobile guns; minotaurs break positions that cannot be bypassed. Shamans draw on remembered migrations and the physical rhythm of collective movement. Their magic helps armies find routes, but does not create food or replacement axles.

Running War grants broad infantry mobility and powerful charges. Poor armour and short effective ranges make exposed advances costly. Raiding is economically necessary for some caravans and opportunistic predation for others; the Exodus contains both liberators and bandits. Its leaders must distinguish a legitimate seizure from an excuse to take a weaker settlement’s winter stores. If they cannot, the road becomes an empire that simply refuses to write down its borders.

A place at the table without a throne
The Exodus shares routes and anti-slavery campaigns with the Cinderjaw Freeholds, but objects when their liberation columns consume more supplies than the freed people can replace. The Synod negotiates seasonal migration through living landscapes, sometimes banning a route to protect an endangered ecosystem. Compact frontier governments vary between welcoming skilled migrants and treating every caravan as an invasion.

The Dominion is especially resented for undermining water routes and turning refuge tunnels into military assets. The Riftbound Ascendancy recruits among displaced northerners, promising the power to destroy every wall. Hornbound elders warn that a pact can be a fence carried inside the body. Their conflict with the Ascendancy therefore concerns what freedom means after escape: the ability to move without permission, or the power to make everyone else move at your command.

The Long Road
A chain of mapped migration corridors across several worlds, connected by leased transport gates. It is recognised as sovereign territory by some powers and as a legal impossibility by others.

Nine-Hearth Basin
A neutral seasonal assembly ground with permanent hospitals and schools. Weapons may be carried, but disputes cannot interrupt access to water.

Stormhoof Steppe
A high-wind world supporting centaur communities and enormous mobile agricultural platforms. Its roads are built to be repaired without central permission.

The Open Hearth
Confederation loyalists defend migration rights and negotiated passage. Their armies favour balanced escorts because a victory is worthless if the civilian wagons are lost.

Stormhoof Circles
Centaur military societies favour mounted fire and rapid pursuit. They resist being treated as transport assets rather than equal political communities.

The Ironhorn Clans
Minotaur builders and breachers specialise in opening roads through hostile fortifications. Their reputation for strength conceals a sophisticated tradition of structural engineering.

The Red Road
Predatory raiding factions claim every settled storehouse represents stolen freedom. The wider Exodus condemns their indiscriminate attacks but struggles to police groups that can simply leave.

Road-Mother Ygra Manypaths
Ygra first led a migration after a government revoked her people’s right to use the river they had irrigated for generations. She negotiated passage through hostile territory by offering bridge-building skills instead of tribute. Her authority depends on maintaining that distinction between cooperation and submission. She is a patient coalition commander who becomes uncompromising when an ally proposes sacrificing the slowest wagons.

Tarek Stormhoof
Tarek was offered a hereditary throne by a Compact client state that wanted his centaur followers to become permanent border cavalry. He refused and led them back onto the road. His dragoons combine accurate moving fire with sudden charges. He believes mobility should serve collective safety, but younger riders admire his victories more than his warnings against personal glory.

Bhorun Gatebreaker
Bhorun learned demolition as a captive construction worker ordered to reinforce a prison wall. He later brought down that wall without collapsing the occupied cells behind it. His reputation is built on precise destruction rather than brute rage. In battle he leads minotaur assaults, while in council he asks who must live beside the ruins after the army has moved on.

54 AC — The Opening of the Camps
Several beastfolk communities coordinated an escape through industrial transport tunnels. Their temporary alliance became the first route assembly.

182 AC — The Bridge of Names
A caravan defended a bridge long enough for an enemy settlement to evacuate. The treaty that followed established the Open Hearth’s principle of reciprocal refuge.

308 AC — The Seventeen Fences
Bhorun’s forces dismantled a chain of fortified labour estates. Red Road raiders then looted the liberated stores, forcing Ygra to fight an internal campaign over the meaning of the victory.

{"sections":[["The north beyond the map","The Riftbound Ascendancy arose in northern systems whose Crown anchors failed outward, opening persistent passages into a dimension of mutable identity. Their people survived by negotiating with entities that could alter flesh, gravity and memory. The first pacts were practical: warmth through a lethal winter, protection from radiation, a navigable path between isolated worlds. Later rulers discovered that the same bargains could purchase conquest.

The Ascendancy is not a single demon cult. It is a hierarchy of mortal jarldoms, covenant hosts and manifested powers bound together by contracts no party entirely trusts. Its ideology teaches that fixed limits are tools of domination and that transformation is the highest form of sovereignty. In practice, the stronger signatory usually writes the terms. A warrior escaping one master may spend the rest of life becoming a weapon for another."],["The law of the pact","Northern communities preserve long oral histories and complex hospitality traditions. Their mortal populations are not uniformly malicious, and many live under covenants inherited from ancestors who faced extinction. The Ascendancy’s ruling warlords exploit these obligations, claiming that successful expansion will eventually buy freedom from the demons. The demons promise the same thing in carefully incompatible language.

Names, scars and witnessed deeds anchor a pact. Chainwrights maintain the machinery that gives a demon physical stability; witches interpret the conditions under which it may act. Mutations can be chosen enhancements, unintended consequences or punishments disguised as gifts. The faction’s deepest social division separates those who want better contracts from those who want to abolish the entire relationship. Neither can easily survive long enough to prove the other wrong."],["An army that changes during the war","Oathscar Reavers and Abyssforged Knights form the disciplined mortal core. Hellwake Riders break lines, while unstable thralls and manifested demons attack where ordinary biology would fail. Pact Furnaces and Breachmouth guns combine real industrial machinery with entities that alter the behaviour of ammunition. Covenants provide cohesion, but every command must account for the motives of the beings carrying it out.

Mutable Flesh increases a formation’s weapon damage as it destroys enemies, rewarding momentum without granting unlimited growth. A commander must feed the right units opportunities while preventing the army from chasing kills instead of securing the field. The faction has strong assault power but inconsistent accuracy and expensive heavy assets. Its political weakness is transactional loyalty: a bad campaign invites subordinates to renegotiate the terms under which they remain subordinate."],["The conquest of possibility","The Ascendancy views the Crown as a prison built to keep reality stable. It seeks enough relays to make transformation permanent and remove the distinction between ordinary space and the realm beyond. This brings it into conflict with nearly every power that depends on predictable physical laws, including the Vesperglass Cabals, whose profitable uncertainty still requires customers to remain recognisable.

Its relationship with the Hollow Star is rivalry rather than simple alliance. The Ascendancy celebrates becoming; the Convent seeks ownership through vows. Demonic beings can serve either, but a patron that appears in both systems will attempt to make the contracts collide. The Daughters oppose both while recognising that a frightened northern civilian is not the same as the warlord who sold that civilian’s future. Hornbound recruiters and Dawn rescue missions threaten the Ascendancy by offering escape without a new supernatural master."]],"worlds":[["Veydr’s Reach","A cold system of oath-halls, industrial fjords and unstable auroral rifts. No map of its interior remains accurate for more than one negotiated passage."],["Chainfall","A forge moon where living smiths and bound entities construct pact engines. Their archives contain examples of disasters caused by a single ambiguous pronoun."],["The Unfinished Host","Manifested demons and enthusiastic transformists reject stable identity. They are powerful assault troops and notoriously poor custodians of conquered infrastructure."],["The Severed Chain","Rebel covenanters seek freedom from inherited pacts. His people admire his courage and have begun to question why the promised release is always one war away. He is an effective combined-arms commander because he understands the limits his speeches deny."],["Myrka of the Ninth Wound","Myrka survived nine supposedly fatal injuries by renegotiating her personal covenant. It regards permanent form as a mortal superstition and takes delight in forcing adversaries to revise their understanding mid-battle. Unlike many patrons it openly admits that its concept of liberation may destroy the people receiving it. Korr respects this honesty more than he should trust the being behind it."]],"wars":[["11 AC — The Winter Bargains","Northern colonies made emergency pacts after their reactors and orbital supplies failed. The north beyond the map
The Riftbound Ascendancy arose in northern systems whose Crown anchors failed outward, opening persistent passages into a dimension of mutable identity. Their people survived by negotiating with entities that could alter flesh, gravity and memory. The first pacts were practical: warmth through a lethal winter, protection from radiation, a navigable path between isolated worlds. Later rulers discovered that the same bargains could purchase conquest.

The Ascendancy is not a single demon cult. It is a hierarchy of mortal jarldoms, covenant hosts and manifested powers bound together by contracts no party entirely trusts. Its ideology teaches that fixed limits are tools of domination and that transformation is the highest form of sovereignty. In practice, the stronger signatory usually writes the terms. A warrior escaping one master may spend the rest of life becoming a weapon for another.

The law of the pact
Northern communities preserve long oral histories and complex hospitality traditions. Their mortal populations are not uniformly malicious, and many live under covenants inherited from ancestors who faced extinction. The Ascendancy’s ruling warlords exploit these obligations, claiming that successful expansion will eventually buy freedom from the demons. The demons promise the same thing in carefully incompatible language.

Names, scars and witnessed deeds anchor a pact. Chainwrights maintain the machinery that gives a demon physical stability; witches interpret the conditions under which it may act. Mutations can be chosen enhancements, unintended consequences or punishments disguised as gifts. The faction’s deepest social division separates those who want better contracts from those who want to abolish the entire relationship. Neither can easily survive long enough to prove the other wrong.

An army that changes during the war
Oathscar Reavers and Abyssforged Knights form the disciplined mortal core. Hellwake Riders break lines, while unstable thralls and manifested demons attack where ordinary biology would fail. Pact Furnaces and Breachmouth guns combine real industrial machinery with entities that alter the behaviour of ammunition. Covenants provide cohesion, but every command must account for the motives of the beings carrying it out.

Mutable Flesh increases a formation’s weapon damage as it destroys enemies, rewarding momentum without granting unlimited growth. A commander must feed the right units opportunities while preventing the army from chasing kills instead of securing the field. The faction has strong assault power but inconsistent accuracy and expensive heavy assets. Its political weakness is transactional loyalty: a bad campaign invites subordinates to renegotiate the terms under which they remain subordinate.

The conquest of possibility
The Ascendancy views the Crown as a prison built to keep reality stable. It seeks enough relays to make transformation permanent and remove the distinction between ordinary space and the realm beyond. This brings it into conflict with nearly every power that depends on predictable physical laws, including the Vesperglass Cabals, whose profitable uncertainty still requires customers to remain recognisable.

Its relationship with the Hollow Star is rivalry rather than simple alliance. The Ascendancy celebrates becoming; the Convent seeks ownership through vows. Demonic beings can serve either, but a patron that appears in both systems will attempt to make the contracts collide. The Daughters oppose both while recognising that a frightened northern civilian is not the same as the warlord who sold that civilian’s future. Hornbound recruiters and Dawn rescue missions threaten the Ascendancy by offering escape without a new supernatural master.

Veydr’s Reach
A cold system of oath-halls, industrial fjords and unstable auroral rifts. Its inhabitants measure seasons by both temperature and the reliability of natural law.

The Ninth Wound
A permanent breach surrounded by covenant fortresses. No map of its interior remains accurate for more than one negotiated passage.

Chainfall
A forge moon where living smiths and bound entities construct pact engines. The oldest factory contract is longer than the city’s legal code.

The Storm Jarldoms
Mortal northern rulers favour disciplined reavers and heavy knights. They claim to command demons as allies while carefully avoiding the question of who can terminate the agreement.

The Ninth Covenant
Witches and jurists believe survival depends on exact interpretation. Their archives contain examples of disasters caused by a single ambiguous pronoun.

The Unfinished Host
Manifested demons and enthusiastic transformists reject stable identity. They are powerful assault troops and notoriously poor custodians of conquered infrastructure.

The Severed Chain
Rebel covenanters seek freedom from inherited pacts. Some fight beside outsiders; others believe only a larger, more destructive bargain can break the old one.

High Jarl Korr Veydr
Korr inherited a kingdom whose winters were kept survivable by a demon demanding annual military service. He expanded that service into a campaign of conquest, insisting each captured relay brings independence closer. His people admire his courage and have begun to question why the promised release is always one war away. He is an effective combined-arms commander because he understands the limits his speeches deny.

Myrka of the Ninth Wound
Myrka survived nine supposedly fatal injuries by renegotiating her personal covenant. Each recovery removed something from her previous identity. She records her decisions in an external journal so that the person she becomes can be held accountable by the person she was. Her magic is formidable, but her real ambition is to discover a form of healing that does not require a creditor.

Tharoz the Unfinished
Tharoz manifests differently to every witness but consistently remembers the promises made to it. It regards permanent form as a mortal superstition and takes delight in forcing adversaries to revise their understanding mid-battle. Unlike many patrons it openly admits that its concept of liberation may destroy the people receiving it. Korr respects this honesty more than he should trust the being behind it.

11 AC — The Winter Bargains
Northern colonies made emergency pacts after their reactors and orbital supplies failed. Later governments converted temporary survival contracts into inherited obligations.

173 AC — The War of Broken Names
A jarl attempted to nullify every covenant by renaming his people. The resulting conflict established that identity was more than a label and considerably harder to escape.

305 AC — The Siege of Chainfall
Rebels nearly destroyed the forge moon’s master contract. Korr saved the factories, then discovered that preserving them had renewed obligations he had intended to end.

factions.history:
The forest that learned to answer
The Verdant Synod arose when Aether currents connected ancient forests, engineered reclamation ecosystems and the people living within them. Some landscapes acquired distributed awareness; others revealed minds that had always existed but lacked a language their neighbours could hear. The first recognised Synod was an agreement between a river basin, three ranger communities and a damaged weather-control network.

This origin makes the faction neither a simple return to nature nor an enemy of all technology. Many of its sacred groves contain deliberate bioengineering, and some treefolk trace their lineage to industrial remediation projects. The Synod judges tools by their place in a living system. A rifle grown from bioceramic tissue is acceptable if its production and use can be sustained. A beautiful garden maintained by draining another world is not innocent merely because its owners prefer leaves to smokestacks.

Many minds, one watershed
A Synod combines local peoples with the landscapes that sustain them. Rangers, treefolk, human settlers and other inhabitants choose Speakers who interpret between individual and distributed minds. Decisions may take hours or decades depending on whether the question concerns a military patrol or the future course of a river. Emergency commanders are therefore granted temporary authority bounded by explicit ecological obligations.

The system can fail through unequal representation. A vast old forest may consider a century a short delay while a village needs medicine tomorrow. Speakers can exploit the difficulty of verifying what a landscape truly said. The Synod trains independent listeners to challenge such claims. Its most important civil right is the right to dissent from communion: joining a shared awareness must not erase the individual or make privacy appear to be treason against the ecosystem.

A war fought through the senses
Rootwatch Rangers and Leafglass Stalkers favour accurate ranged fire, concealed movement and target denial. Thornbound Wardens defend chokepoints, while Briarhart Riders exploit routes heavy machines cannot use efficiently. Groveheart Colossi provide durable fire support at the cost of slow replacement. Sporefall artillery attacks from behind cover, and Cantors coordinate magic through living networks.

Living Veil gives infantry persistent cover and additional movement when starting in physical cover. The force can evade and endure shooting better than its thin armour suggests, but close assault and cover-ignoring weapons remain dangerous. Biological logistics are not effortless: living ammunition needs nutrients, colossi need recovery time and a damaged ecosystem cannot simply be ordered to increase production. The Synod’s commanders must decide how much of the world they can consume while claiming to defend it.

The boundaries of restoration
The Synod trades food and medicines with the Compact and negotiates migration routes with the Hornbound. It fights the Kharad over destructive mining yet buys carefully limited tools from their most scrupulous guilds. Sauridian solar engineering can restore damaged climates, but the Dynasty sometimes assumes that old stewardship grants present ownership.

The Dominion represents a concealed ecological threat because a surface forest can appear healthy while its water systems are being diverted below. The Hollow Star corrupts the meaning of communion by turning shared feeling into compulsory devotion. The Synod’s own extremists can commit a related error: treating the restoration of an ideal landscape as permission to remove the people currently living there. The best Speakers insist that a world’s memory includes its cities, scars and newcomers, not only the version they find easiest to love.

Everdusk Basin
A continent-sized watershed whose distributed mind changes emphasis with the seasons. Its capital is a moving assembly rather than a permanent throne.

The Glassleaf Reaches
Forests adapted to industrial contaminants now produce useful optical fibres. Their existence complicates any claim that healing means restoring an untouched past.

Seven Springs
A world whose seven surviving water systems each elect a Speaker through different customs. Thalen’s people preserve the memory of a failed attempt to merge them by force.

Rootwatch Communes
Settled ranger communities favour patient defence and negotiated ecological limits. They are skilled at preserving territory but sometimes reluctant to aid distant landscapes.

The Leafglass Hunt
Mobile scouts and marksmen disrupt enemy logistics. Their doctrine avoids unnecessary destruction, though isolated cells can become unaccountable judges of what is necessary.

The Deep Communion
Treefolk and Cantors cultivate large-scale shared awareness. Their political challenge is respecting short-lived people whose needs cannot wait for a forest’s deliberation.

The Cinderseed Covenant
Restoration specialists work in ruined industrial worlds rather than pristine groves. Traditionalists call their hybrid ecosystems impure; survivors call them habitable.

Speaker Naeva Rootsong
Naeva grew up in a mining settlement blamed for poisoning the forest beside it. She uncovered evidence that an upstream concession had diverted the treatment funds and persuaded both communities to defend the evidence together. Chosen as Speaker by people and forest alike, she treats translation as a duty to reveal disagreement, not conceal it. Her armies coordinate rifle fire and patient territorial defence.

Elder Thalen of Seven Springs
Thalen participated in an early Synod campaign that redirected a river to restore one sacred grove and destroyed several downstream communities. He has spent centuries opposing the belief that ecological scale makes individual suffering irrelevant. His great body is a formidable war engine, but his counsel is cautious. He remembers that an army can sincerely protect life while making terrible decisions about which lives count.

Hunt-Marshal Sira Leafglass
Sira commands dispersed ranger cells through signals too quiet for most machines to distinguish from weather. She prefers to disable depots and transport routes rather than attack settlements. Her restraint is strategic as well as ethical: a civilian who can live after the war is less likely to become the next enemy. Her hunters have repeatedly exposed Dominion water theft beneath apparently untouched forests.

33 AC — The First Answering
A damaged river-control network began speaking through nearby roots. Its negotiated repair became the founding agreement of the modern Synod.

156 AC — The Misguided Spring
An attempt to restore one ecosystem by force ruined another. The resulting inquiry established independent listeners and a formal right to refuse communion.

304 AC — The Glassleaf Recovery
Rangers and industrial refugees rebuilt a poisoned region into a stable hybrid forest. The campaign remains a political argument about whether recovery must resemble the past.

factions.history:
Custodians of an unfinished dawn
The Sauridian Helion Dynasty inhabits temple-cities built around ancient solar engines. Its reptilian peoples preserve biological and astronomical records older than any present human state, but age has not made those records complete. The Dynasty believes it was entrusted with maintaining a network that once regulated climates and star routes. Its oldest inscriptions describe a duty without clearly identifying the authority that assigned it.

For centuries the rulers interpreted stewardship as obedience to a sacred timetable. The Crown fracture made that certainty impossible. Some engines continued to operate while their appointed skies no longer matched the predictions. Others demanded actions that would harm the populations they were supposed to sustain. The modern Dynasty is divided between those who believe the custodians have misunderstood the instructions and those who believe the instructions themselves must now be changed.

Broods and civic purpose
Sauridian society combines several reptilian lineages adapted to different environments and tasks. Broods are educational and kinship communities, not an absolute caste system. Small-bodied Glassfins often become scouts, broad Shellguards favour heavy work and defence, and crest-bearing cohorts supply much of the line army. Individuals can cross these traditions, though old temple houses do not always make it easy.

The Sun-Regent is chosen through a combination of brood councils, military evaluation and astromantic examination. Succession disputes arise when these methods disagree. Hatcheries are treated as civic institutions, and their protection is one of the few priorities capable of uniting rival temples immediately. The Dynasty’s long lives encourage careful planning, but can also make leaders underestimate the urgency felt by younger allies. A promise to return in forty years is not comforting to a settlement under attack today.

Reliable strength, living engines
Sunscale infantry are durable and predictable, making the Dynasty a forgiving army to learn. Crestguard defend the command network; Glassfins scout; raptor riders supply a mobile assault arm. Solarback Behemoths and regulated salamander breeds carry biological weapons integrated with mechanical stabilisers. The animals are trained and cared for as valuable partners, although the degree of genuine respect varies between temple houses.

Brood Resonance reinforces infantry armour and objective control near a commander. It represents disciplined signalling and Aether-assisted coordination, not complete mind control. The army grows less efficient when spread too widely or when leaders are removed. Heavy beasts require food, veterinary care and suitable transport; solar systems need stored energy when local conditions are poor. Stable scaling comes from maintaining those supports, not from limitless monsters appearing without an ecological cost.

The burden of inheritance
The Dynasty shares astronomical research with the Lumen Arc but dislikes decisions justified by futures that can be rewritten after the fact. It trades durable ceramics and climate machinery with the Compact and Kharad. Relations with the Synod are productive when stewardship is negotiated and hostile when a temple declares itself owner of a living world because an ancient engine stands there.

Verminhorde engineers covet the solar reactors and biological archives. The Dynasty fears theft not merely as lost equipment but as a misuse of a system whose larger purpose remains uncertain. The Riftbound want to transform the engines; the Hollow Star wants to make worship their fuel. Sauridian reformers argue that the custodians’ real task is to protect living people from inherited machinery when necessary. Traditionalists consider that argument the first step toward abandoning the only duty that gives their civilisation meaning.

Helion Prime
The central temple-world contains the First Meridian, a solar engine that has never stopped running even though no one can fully explain what it powers.

Xala’s Crown
A warm archipelago world whose brood cities integrate hatcheries, colleges and raptor reserves. Its civic architecture is deliberately accessible to several body plans.

The Obsidian March
A volcanic frontier of ancient relay sites and armoured megafauna. Temple expeditions compete to interpret newly exposed inscriptions before rivals claim them.

The First Meridian
Orthodox temples favour reliable cohorts, heavy guardians and strict command cohesion. Their strengths become liabilities when old procedures no longer fit new conditions.

The Open Sun
Reformist brood councils advocate adapting the ancient duty to present lives. They field mixed forces and welcome technical exchanges with other peoples.

The Raptor Courts
Mounted traditions specialise in reconnaissance and decisive charges. Their honour codes emphasise care for mounts, though competitive prestige can still encourage reckless losses.

The Deep Observatory
Astromancers preserve long records and investigate the engines’ hidden connections. Their secrecy protects dangerous knowledge and sometimes prevents necessary correction.

Sun-Regent Xalatek
Xalatek was selected after ordering a ceremonial engine shut down when its activation threatened a populated valley. The successful shutdown saved the valley and erased the only surviving record of the engine’s intended purpose. He now rules a people divided over whether he fulfilled or betrayed their inheritance. His battlefield leadership is steady, building strong formations around an intact command network.

Crest-Marshal Issara Venn
Issara’s raptor formations combine inherited hunting signals with modern communications. She rose by defending a hatchery without waiting for a temple council to complete its jurisdictional debate. Her popularity among younger broods makes conservative rulers uneasy. She believes tradition earns respect by remaining useful and has no patience for commanders who treat avoidable casualties as proof of devotion.

Star-Reader Oq-Telan
Oq-Telan discovered a persistent drift in the Dynasty’s sacred timetable. He initially concealed it while checking the instruments, then realised that several earlier readers had done the same. His present mission is to recover those suppressed observations. He commands powerful Aether disciplines but distrusts revelations that cannot be compared against physical evidence.

Before 0 AC — The Custodial Ages
Surviving records establish solar maintenance traditions long before the fracture, but disagree about the identity of the original builders. The uncertainty is part of the setting, not a solved origin.

91 AC — The Silent Meridian
A temple followed an ancient activation schedule and found that its promised star route no longer existed. The loss created the first organised reform movement.

303 AC — The Hatchery War
Issara held a brood world against raiders while its government debated command authority. Her victory forced the Dynasty to recognise emergency action without hereditary permission.

factions.name: Daughters of the Unbroken Dawn
factions.motto: No life is beneath the light.
factions.description: An all-female holy military order. Armoured sisters, healing saints and radiant engines defend the helpless without demanding conversion.
factions.lore:
{"sections":[["The covenant of the unbroken light","The Daughters of the Unbroken Dawn are an all-female holy military order founded after a catastrophe known as the Long Eclipse. When a relay failure darkened several inhabited worlds, hospitals and evacuation stations became the first targets of desperate armies. A network of women physicians, engineers, guards and spiritual teachers formed mutual-defence houses around those refuges. Their first sacred promise was practical: no wounded person would be surrendered to an aggressor because helping them was politically inconvenient.

The earliest miracles occurred during the defence of a refuge whose generators had failed. Witnesses described a steady light that protected the shelter without burning those outside it. The Daughters call its source the Unbroken Light, a benevolent transcendence that answers freely undertaken acts of protection. They do not claim to own it. Their theology holds that a miracle obtained through coercion is already something else, regardless of how radiant it appears."],["Women sworn to shelter","Every sworn member of the faction is a woman: commanders, rifle sisters, scouts, pilots, artillery crews, engineers, healers and living saints. Recruitment is voluntary and open across human cultures and social backgrounds. The order’s women-only covenant is its institutional tradition, not a claim that other people are lesser or incapable of holiness. Allied men and nonmembers may receive protection, employment or political representation in the communities it serves, but are not disguised male combat units within its roster.

The Houses of Shelter elect a High Matriarch for a fixed term. Independent sisters called Witnesses audit conduct, finances and the treatment of prisoners. A sister may challenge an unlawful command without forfeiting her vows. Leaving the order is permitted after an orderly transfer of duties. Their discipline is demanding because goodness requires responsibility, but it does not depend on humiliating penitents, forced conversion or manufacturing martyrs."],["Faith expressed through action","Dawn devotion is measured by truthful conduct, care for the vulnerable and restraint toward a defeated enemy. Their holy character is genuine within the setting. They are not secretly another predatory empire waiting for a darker reveal. This does not make them omniscient. Sisters can misjudge evidence, exhaust supplies or disagree bitterly over which threatened community they can reach first. Their moral struggle concerns limited power and conflicting duties, rather than a hidden conviction that cruelty is virtue.

Miracles require coherent Aether, trained intention and a freely accepted burden. They cannot be mass-produced by ordering civilians to pray. Hospitals therefore keep ordinary medicine, factories maintain spare parts and quartermasters plan for miracles to fail. Saints are examined by Witnesses rather than granted absolute authority. The order honours those who die protecting others while teaching that surviving to protect again is not a lesser form of courage."],["Armour, flame and mercy","The army combines disciplined armoured sisters with radiant firearms, shield units, mobile lancers and carefully controlled artillery. Purifying Flame Sisters destroy demonic anchors and dangerous war materiel; their doctrine forbids treating an inhabited district as a convenient cleansing target. Sanctuary Engines carry women crews and practical rescue equipment. Saints and Sisters of the Living Light support the same soldiers who maintain the order’s mundane defence network.
