factions.history:
The covenant of the unbroken light
The Daughters of the Unbroken Dawn are an all-female holy military order founded after a catastrophe known as the Long Eclipse. When a relay failure darkened several inhabited worlds, hospitals and evacuation stations became the first targets of desperate armies. A network of women physicians, engineers, guards and spiritual teachers formed mutual-defence houses around those refuges. Their first sacred promise was practical: no wounded person would be surrendered to an aggressor because helping them was politically inconvenient.

The earliest miracles occurred during the defence of a refuge whose generators had failed. Witnesses described a steady light that protected the shelter without burning those outside it. The Daughters call its source the Unbroken Light, a benevolent transcendence that answers freely undertaken acts of protection. They do not claim to own it. Their theology holds that a miracle obtained through coercion is already something else, regardless of how radiant it appears.

Women sworn to shelter
Every sworn member of the faction is a woman: commanders, rifle sisters, scouts, pilots, artillery crews, engineers, healers and living saints. Recruitment is voluntary and open across human cultures and social backgrounds. The order’s women-only covenant is its institutional tradition, not a claim that other people are lesser or incapable of holiness. Allied men and nonmembers may receive protection, employment or political representation in the communities it serves, but are not disguised male combat units within its roster.

The Houses of Shelter elect a High Matriarch for a fixed term. Independent sisters called Witnesses audit conduct, finances and the treatment of prisoners. A sister may challenge an unlawful command without forfeiting her vows. Leaving the order is permitted after an orderly transfer of duties. Their discipline is demanding because goodness requires responsibility, but it does not depend on humiliating penitents, forced conversion or manufacturing martyrs.

Faith expressed through action
Dawn devotion is measured by truthful conduct, care for the vulnerable and restraint toward a defeated enemy. Their holy character is genuine within the setting. They are not secretly another predatory empire waiting for a darker reveal. This does not make them omniscient. Sisters can misjudge evidence, exhaust supplies or disagree bitterly over which threatened community they can reach first. Their moral struggle concerns limited power and conflicting duties, rather than a hidden conviction that cruelty is virtue.

Miracles require coherent Aether, trained intention and a freely accepted burden. They cannot be mass-produced by ordering civilians to pray. Hospitals therefore keep ordinary medicine, factories maintain spare parts and quartermasters plan for miracles to fail. Saints are examined by Witnesses rather than granted absolute authority. The order honours those who die protecting others while teaching that surviving to protect again is not a lesser form of courage.

Armour, flame and mercy
The army combines disciplined armoured sisters with radiant firearms, shield units, mobile lancers and carefully controlled artillery. Purifying Flame Sisters destroy demonic anchors and dangerous war materiel; their doctrine forbids treating an inhabited district as a convenient cleansing target. Sanctuary Engines carry women crews and practical rescue equipment. Saints and Sisters of the Living Light support the same soldiers who maintain the order’s mundane defence network.

Merciful Radiance makes protective Ward magic cheaper, improves nearby recovery from suppression and grants Benediction healing. This creates a resilient combined-arms force, but it remains expensive and can be outnumbered. Aether shortages, anti-armour fire and divided rescue obligations create real weaknesses. In the current battle game the artillery still uses the common blast rules, including friendly fire; holiness does not exempt the player from responsible targeting.

The wound called the Hollow Star
The Hollow Star began with a faction of sisters who decided that protection should confer ownership and that withheld miracles justified stealing power. The Daughters remember the betrayal without treating every survivor as permanently beyond rescue. They offer surrender to mortals who can still choose freely, while opposing the Convent’s leaders and predatory manifestations without romanticising them.

The Daughters cooperate with the Compact, Hornbound, Synod and others when civilian lives can be protected. They will also oppose those allies if the alliance demands atrocity. The Continuum’s consensual restoration is debated respectfully rather than automatically condemned as evil; the relevant question is whether the person remains free. Their strongest strategic asset is trust built through costly consistency. Their enemies exploit that trust by creating multiple emergencies, knowing the sisters cannot simply stop caring when care becomes inconvenient.

Aster’s Refuge
The original hospital-world now holds the order’s principal Witness council. Its central sanctuary has doors facing every landing field and no private entrance for dignitaries.

Dawnward Bastion
A fortress and evacuation port built to shelter populations rather than merely garrison troops. Its outer defences can be sacrificed without cutting off the hospital districts.

The Lantern Pilgrimage
A network of mobile relief fleets and small houses on endangered worlds. Many sisters spend their entire service here without visiting the ceremonial capital.

Order of the Open Hand
Healers and protective infantry prioritise evacuation, medicine and prisoner safety. They are sometimes accused of surrendering tactical advantage to obligations other armies would ignore.

Order of the Vigilant Sword
Armoured battle sisters specialise in disciplined counterattack against threats to protected communities. Their internal debates concern when pre-emptive force is truly necessary.

Order of the Far Lantern
Scouts, pilots and mounted sisters defend remote routes. Their isolation demands independent judgement and makes reliable evidence more precious than impressive doctrine.

Order of the Unbroken Seal
Artificers, wardsmiths and exo-armour crews contain demonic breaches. They train specifically to distinguish corruption from unfamiliar but harmless spiritual traditions.

The Witness Houses
Independent investigators serve throughout the order. Their authority to question saints and matriarchs is treated as a sacred protection against the return of Vaelora’s error.

High Matriarch Elyra Solenne
Elyra was a surgeon during a war in which both sides claimed her hospital’s patients as enemies. She armed its evacuation teams and refused to release either group to execution. Elected Matriarch for her judgement rather than miraculous power, she regards every battle plan as a list of lives entrusted to her. Her public disagreements with Serene are preserved in the order’s archives so that future sisters can learn how principled people resolve competing duties.

Marshal Serene Valecourt
Serene commands the order’s largest field host. She once abandoned a near-certain pursuit victory to recover prisoners from a collapsing enemy transport, allowing the defeated commander to escape. Critics still invoke the decision; the rescued people do too. She is neither naive nor gentle toward an active threat. Her skill lies in using overwhelming local force without allowing the convenience of violence to decide its proper limits.

Saint-Errant Iona Vey
Iona’s first recorded miracle restored light to an evacuation corridor while she remained behind to guide the last wounded through it. She refuses permanent command because she fears people will obey her radiance when they should examine her reasoning. Her power is strongest in direct protection and healing. She travels with ordinary supply crews and insists that the names of the women who repair her transport appear beside hers in mission records.

62 AC — The Long Eclipse
Refuge houses formed a mutual-defence covenant during a cascade of relay failures. The first shelter miracle became the order’s spiritual foundation.

198 AC — The Broken Benediction
Vaelora’s faction attempted to compel miracles through an oath-engine. The resulting schism created the Hollow Star and forced the Daughters to formalise independent Witness oversight.

307 AC — The Shelter of Unpaid Names
Sisters defended escaped memory debtors against Vesperglass claims. The campaign established a protected testimony archive that charges no price for a person’s own history.

312 AC — The Dawnward Vigil
Elyra divides her forces between sealing a demonic breach and rescuing civilians deliberately trapped to draw her away. The operation is a current campaign premise, not a predestined victory.

Affection can exist between individuals, but the state continually turns intimacy and trust into instruments of leverage.

The theology of the hollow
The Convent teaches that the universe recognises only successful claims. A blessing is a resource, a soul is a reservoir of possible futures, and mercy is merely the stage before a beneficiary understands the price. Its rituals invert the Dawn’s protections: confession becomes reconnaissance, sanctuary becomes dependency, and an oath freely given is rewritten to survive the giver’s refusal. Its miracles are real in effect and corrupt in source. Soulfire can mend the caster by harming another; possessed armour can preserve a soldier while gradually changing what she wants preserved. The Convent’s most closely guarded secret is how much of its apparent sovereignty is already collateral.

The army of stolen grace
Hollow-Vow Sisters form a disciplined armoured core. Thorned Halo elites assault weakened positions; Veil Confessors sabotage trust and identify targets; Reliquary Sisters endure inside possessed exo-armour. Mourningstar Cavaliers and the Cathedral of Want give the order a distinct mounted and heavy demonic arm. Its guns, incense projectors and artillery are maintained by trained women artificers, so the army remains dangerous even when a ritual fails.

Stolen Benediction rewards enemy destruction with Aether, while Soulfire turns offensive magic into limited self-healing. The faction is encouraged to sustain pressure and finish vulnerable targets. The empire inside a promise

The Continuum attacks its soul machinery; the Synod resists compulsory communion; the Compact struggles against its influence among abandoned citizens. Nox Vespera
A fortress-world built around the First Hollow Engine. Its black chapels imitate places of refuge while routing every oath toward central reservoirs.

A fleet of mobile convent-fortresses that offers military aid to collapsing governments. The landing of its relief ships is often celebrated before anyone reads the terms.

The Unsainted Choir
A breached relay complex where female daemon-saints acquire stable form. Each manifestation changes the architecture to reflect what its patron believes devotion should cost.

The Thorned Halo
Vaelora’s ruling convent favours elite infantry, public ritual and tightly controlled political dependence. It insists the other orders exist only because it permits them to.

The Iron Lament
Sabeth’s professional war-sisters emphasise armour, guns and reliable logistics. They resent ecstatic waste but remain willing participants in the order’s coercive empire.

Infiltrator-priestesses acquire secrets, recruit compromised officials and prepare populations for dependency. Their power depends on keeping some promises while concealing the price of others.

The Unsainted Choir
Daemon-saints and their female attendants seek deeper transformation. They increasingly question why a formerly mortal abbess should command beings she claims to have liberated from human limits.

The Black Reliquary
Fleshsmiths and possessed veterans preserve damaged sisters inside ritual armour. Their workshops are places of remarkable technical care and systematic spiritual captivity.

Abbess-Maledict Vaelora Nox

She now challenges Vaelora’s authority while offering followers an even more intimate form of captivity. Her Soulfire sustains her by consuming the possibilities of the wounded.

Vaelora’s forced miracle severed her faction from the Dawn. The survivors chose to preserve the engine rather than free the lives bound inside it.

257 AC — The Mercy of Nox Vespera
A threatened world accepted permanent military protection. Its government survived, but every subsequent attempt to end the treaty was interpreted as sacrilege.

311 AC — The Last Door Defeat
Continuum forces destroyed a soul refinery and released its captives. Sabeth withdrew in good order while Vaelora publicly denied that anything valuable had been lost.

312 AC — The Unsainted Succession
Morwenna’s growing influence divides the Convent between human command and daemon sovereignty. The crisis is unresolved and supplies several possible campaign directions.

factions.history:
The volunteers who inherited a debt
The first Testament was a list of civilians stranded outside a sealed orbital shelter. Its military governor had followed every evacuation regulation and still abandoned sixty thousand people. The surviving rescue crews did not overthrow him. They placed his own orders beside the names of the dead and demanded a law under which obedience could no longer excuse abandonment. Their descendants now carry that law into battle. The Argent Testament recruits adults who have already served civilian rescue institutions. Augmentation buys the endurance needed to remain on a failing world after ordinary forces must depart; it is neither an inherited caste nor proof of moral superiority.

The making of a witness
A candidate spends seven years as a witness before receiving the dense skeletal lattice and redundant circulation of a full soldier. Most candidates become medics, navigators or advocates instead. Each completed warrior accepts a testament: the recorded testimony of a person who died because a system failed. It must be recited accurately, including criticism of the military. These voices are private obligations rather than a collective consciousness. Some soldiers have discovered that their cherished testimonies were edited, and the resulting crisis of trust has become the order’s deepest internal conflict.

Houses, courts and command
The Argent houses are mobile institutions: a rescue fleet, a regiment and a court travelling together. A commander can order a retreat, but must submit its reasoning to civilian witnesses afterwards. The First Listener coordinates campaigns without owning the houses. Their autonomy makes them unusually resistant to a single corrupt ruler and painfully slow when several legitimate obligations conflict. Officers wear blank ivory faceplates on duty so that testimony concerns the decision rather than the celebrity of the person making it. Names are spoken openly at the subsequent inquiry.

Arms of the long vigil
Testament armour is a repairable pressure hull, plated with pale ceramic and supported by copper load frames. Coil weapons favour precise bursts over spectacular expenditure. Shield files establish safe corridors while breach cadres destroy strongpoints and heavy escorts carry civilians out through the breach. Choirwrights use Aether to hold failing structures together; the same geometry can pin an enemy formation. The Last Witness, a walking archive protected by overlapping shield vanes, anchors these operations. Its immense defensive field is strongest around nearby infantry, making separation a deliberate counter to an otherwise formidable battle line.

Allies who do not agree
The Daughters of the Unbroken Dawn welcome the Testament’s refusal to abandon the vulnerable, but dispute its insistence that every revelation remain open to evidence. Compact governments value the houses until an inquiry reaches a politically useful officer. Vault auditors admire their contracts and distrust their willingness to incur impossible debts. The Oathscar Reclaimers claim to be the only honest heirs of the original rescue crews: they argue that the dead demand conquest rather than testimony. Argent commanders must resist turning a defence of the living into a war to silence that accusation.

The quiet beyond the relays
Three houses vanished after entering a region where distress calls continued but human voices had ceased. The last surviving transmission contained a perfectly ordinary maintenance checklist spoken in the voices of several long-dead witnesses. The Testament calls this phenomenon the Quiet Dread. An investigation is underway, but commanders disagree over whether the silent worlds contain people awaiting rescue or a mechanism learning how to ask for it. The player’s expedition is authorised to recover evidence, protect living populations and refuse orders that cannot survive public accounting.

Orison Anchorage
A ring of rescue docks around a cold ocean world. Its civilian courts meet in the same halls used to assemble expeditionary armour, so testimony is heard above the sound of repairs. No house may own a permanent seat.

The White Causeway
A chain of pressure shelters spanning a shattered moon. Each shelter is named for the people who maintained it during the original evacuation. Training expeditions must cross the entire chain while repairing, rather than merely overcoming, its failures.

Sable Hospice
A neutral station treating veterans from several hostile powers. Testament protection is conditional on disarmament within its hull. The station has become a fragile diplomatic channel precisely because the order refuses to make recovery depend on political obedience.

House of the Open Door
Specialists in breached habitats and contested evacuations. Their commanders insist on identifying an exit route before approving an assault. Shield files, field restorers and the Last Witness protect the resulting corridor.

House of Difficult Evidence
Investigators and reconnaissance troops who recover records from hostile territory. They are respected by civilians and disliked by officers whose reputations depend on convenient gaps in an archive.

The Copper Vigil
Engine crews responsible for the order’s oldest armour. They argue that a repaired machine should retain visible evidence of its failures. Copper seams and exposed replacement plates are therefore marks of responsibility rather than shame.

First Listener Cael Orison
A veteran rescue pilot elected after refusing a ceremonial triumph. Orison links widely separated units through careful fire discipline. He worries that his reputation for restraint now prevents subordinates from reporting situations that require violence.

Breach-Marshal Iona Vey
An engineer who survived the collapse of a station she had certified safe. Vey leads from the breach, retaining every failed structural calculation as a lesson rather than destroying the evidence. Her assault cadre treats speed as a means of rescue, never an end in itself.

Choirwright Sen Aravel
A former acoustic archivist able to hear the deformation of metal through Aether. Aravel believes the silent relay signals are altered testimony and insists on preserving them, despite pressure from officers who would destroy the transmitters.

The Hearing at Meridian Nine
An Argent expedition discovers that a Compact governor fabricated a distress call to obtain military support. The governor’s enemies then attack real evacuation ships. Saving those ships while preserving evidence against their owner becomes the campaign’s central dilemma.

The Last Unedited Voice
Oathscar notaries seize the only surviving original record of the corridor bargain. Three Argent houses disagree over whether rescuing the archive’s living custodians justifies sacrificing the document that might free millions from the Reclaimers’ debt claims.

factions.history:
The unpayable rescue
The Reclaimers descend from an expedition that remained inside a collapsing relay corridor to evacuate a chain of mining worlds. Their command petitioned for relief until its reactors failed. Something beyond the corridor answered with power, and the expedition survived by promising to return every life it had saved. The officers believed the language symbolic. When evacuees began vanishing from their new homes, they learned that the promise had acquired a creditor. Instead of repudiating the bargain, the surviving command declared that it would conquer enough lives to pay the debt.

An empire of substitutions
Oathscar holdings operate through substitution: another worker serves your term, another household pays your levy, another world answers your distress call. Powerful debt houses accumulate layers of proxies until no one can identify the original obligation. The population is not uniformly fanatical. Some inhabitants believe that punctual payment protects them from worse horrors; others hide fugitives or sabotage the ledgers. Reclaimer officers call these acts selfish because an unpaid debt falls on someone else. Their entire moral system makes solidarity appear dangerous while presenting organised cruelty as responsible administration.

The creditor without a face
The entity called the Unwritten Creditor has never issued a clear command. Its agents appear as gaps in records, shadows wearing the posture of absent people and signatures that move between documents. Different warbands disagree over its intentions. The Notaries believe it measures suffering, the Red Executors believe it rewards successful conquest, and the Empty Choir believes that fulfilling every debt will erase the universe. These beliefs produce very different armies, but each finds convenient evidence in victories bought at other people’s expense.

The surviving legions
Reclaimer armour retains the layered engineering of the rescue era, beneath violet seal wax and iron contract plates. Their ammunition carries fragments of binding formulae that tear the firer as well as the target. Veteran files deliberately close the distance so that stolen vitality can repair their wounds. Bound engines are inhabited by entire defaulting households, their conflicting voices channelled into propulsion. The Covenant Eater is the largest of these engines: a titan whose attack consumes its own armour to project a devastating blood contract. It can be worn down by denying it kills and forcing it to cross open ground.

The right to refuse
The Argent Testament preserves copies of the expedition’s original relief requests. Those documents prove both the abandonment and the absence of consent from the rescued populations. This makes the Testament a threat beyond its military strength. Hollow Star convents offer the Reclaimers rituals that cancel individual obligations by sacrificing communities; some debt houses accept, while others consider it an unlawful distortion of their bargain. The Verminhorde trades recovered identities to Oathscar notaries but never grants them access to the All-Mother’s genealogical archives.

A schism waiting for a voice
A growing movement of scarred infantry has begun writing the word Refused across contract plates. They do not deny what happened in the corridor. They reject the claim that survival created the right to own everyone else. No rebellion has yet endured, because liberated settlements often remain dependent on the same engines that enforce the debts. A Reclaimer campaign therefore contains a persistent contradiction: its strongest victories extend a system that even many of its own soldiers secretly want to end.

The Court of Arrears
A city built around a rescue ship that never completed its final docking sequence. Its population lives in compartments labelled with the names of creditors rather than streets. Public clocks count obligations instead of hours.

Vowfall
A world of contract foundries where armour plates are stamped with inherited debts. The foundries employ living workers alongside bound engines containing the voices of former owners. Production interruptions are treated as moral failures.

The Unregistered March
A belt of settlements deliberately omitted from official ledgers. Refugees try to survive without entering any bargain the Creditor might enforce. Reclaimer officers deny these settlements exist while repeatedly requisitioning troops to destroy them.

The Red Executors
Assault cadres who believe a debt becomes legitimate through the strength required to collect it. Their officers encourage close combat because stolen vitality immediately repairs the wounds inflicted by their own weapons.

The Margin Notaries
Sorcerers who alter the interpretation of existing bargains rather than inventing new ones. A missing comma, an erased witness or an ambiguous name may be enough to bind a living formation to an engine.

The Refusal Cells
Underground groups within veteran regiments who preserve evidence of coerced contracts. They remain enemies on the battlefield, but their existence offers a story route toward revolt rather than treating every Reclaimer as incapable of choice.

Executor Mael Rusk
The last surviving officer to sign the corridor bargain. Rusk remembers the exact number of people saved and cannot bear to admit that his effort to honour them has become a greater disaster. His orders drive relentless close-range fire.

Lady Nerezza Vow-Eater
A duellist who purchased her first command by taking the debts of an entire city. Each victory adds another name to her armour. She regards compassion as a weakness in the wording of a contract and seeks opponents whose defeat will prove it.

Notary Ossian Null
A sorcerer whose body was erased from every official register. Null speaks through a mask suspended above an empty pressure suit and uses stolen signatures to turn battlefield casualties into regenerative power.

The City That Paid Twice
A liberated city presents proof that its debt was settled generations earlier. Two Reclaimer houses each insist that the payment belongs to the other’s account. Their rivalry turns into a siege in which the population is punished for possessing accurate records.

The Unwritten Campaign
Ossian Null follows a sequence of victories absent from every military archive. The missing campaigns appear to have created obligations that even the Creditor’s most faithful servants cannot explain. Null intends to own that uncertainty before anyone can resolve it.

factions.history:
The ocean that learned to travel
The Pelagic Hunger began in the ice-covered ocean of a rogue planet. Its organisms exchanged inherited chemical memories through feeding, symbiosis and dissolved signals. When the planet crossed a damaged relay, part of that ecosystem was carried into orbit. The surviving colony adapted to vacuum by growing mineral shells around seawater cavities. Over many migrations these shells became living ships. What other peoples call a single invader is a travelling sea containing thousands of interdependent species and several incompatible plans for survival.

Memory without a throne
Pelagic intelligence has no permanent central monarch. Consensus forms around memory knots: organisms able to retain and compare many generations of chemical experience. A knot can split, merge or be consumed by its own descendants. The hunger of the whole does not make individual bodies disposable in quite the way enemies assume. Every loss removes a unique interpretation of inherited memory. Yet the ecology has no innate concept of an individual right to refuse assimilation, and can commit catastrophic violence while understanding itself to be preserving what it consumes.

The three currents
The Sheltering Current incorporates other life slowly, attempting symbiosis before consumption. The Red Current sees delay as extinction and turns entire biospheres into migration fuel. The Deep Current pursues signals from beyond the relay network, cultivating forms that can survive conditions no scout has described. These tendencies are not political parties; they are competing chemical habits within the same colony. A commander can change allegiance after feeding on new memories, making diplomatic agreements difficult but not meaningless.

Bodies built for a question
Pelagic troops are grown for local conditions. Shoal organisms carry needle sacs and exchange range information through colour. Reefguards concentrate mineral armour around vulnerable signal organs. Harrowers break vehicles with paired limbs, while pressure-spitters fire self-sealing pods of corrosive material. Their great titan, the Abyssal Nursery, is a mobile habitat rather than a solitary predator. It digests battlefield remains to mend itself and releases young organisms into surrounding cells. Destroying its support knots or denying it access to casualties interrupts the feedback that makes a successful advance increasingly difficult to stop.

The taste of another civilisation
The Verdant Synod recognises an ecology in the Hunger but opposes its assumption that all life should share one sea. Sauridian keepers have recorded Pelagic enzymes matching ancient maintenance organisms, an unsettling clue to the Crown’s origin. Verminhorde memory harvesting is superficially familiar to the colonies; the resemblance has produced both exchanges and spectacular misunderstandings. An All-Mother is a sovereign person, not an exposed memory knot, and Dominion diplomacy has had to make that distinction with artillery.

Signals under the silence
Where human receivers hear the Quiet Dread as silence, Pelagic organisms register a persistent pressure gradient. The Deep Current believes something vast is drawing energy away from the relays. It grows bodies with senses aimed at that absence and sends them into the dark. Whether these migrations are investigation, courtship or an attempt to flee is unresolved even within the colonies. Their wars in inhabited systems are both an immediate threat and evidence of a larger ecological disturbance.

The Mother Sea
The rogue planet’s ocean remains a powerful memory rather than a reachable capital. Different colonies carry mutually incompatible accounts of its location. Attempts to reconcile them can trigger changes in the organisms that inherited those accounts.

Shell of the Third Crossing
A living migration vessel large enough to contain several internal seas. Its outer surface is a reef of mineral armour and dormant feeding organs. Human observers first mistook it for a moon with an unexpectedly regular orbit.

The Listening Shoals
Colonies established around submerged relay ruins on an inhabited ocean world. Their slow exchanges with local coastal communities have produced the closest thing to stable diplomacy between the Hunger and another civilisation.

The Sheltering Current
Colonies that seek symbiosis before consumption. Their patience is not unconditional kindness: they still understand separate living systems as incomplete relationships waiting to be joined.

The Red Current
A migration habit shaped by repeated famine. It rewards fast assimilation and aggressive concentration of biomass. Its commanders view every delayed meal as a threat to the lives entrusted to them.

The Deep Current
Exploratory colonies growing senses for the energy gradient behind the Quiet Dread. Their strange bodies can appear inefficient in ordinary combat because they are built to survive a journey whose destination remains unknown.

First Current Sere
A consensus knot carrying the memory of the first successful journey through vacuum. Sere advances cautiously, using cheap bodies to measure threats before committing the colony’s irreplaceable organs.

The Ninth Appetite
A predator whose successive bodies have each survived starvation. It favours violent concentration, breaking a single line before spreading through the breach. Its memories increasingly equate resistance with nourishment.

Lattice-Mother Oru
A symbiotic intelligence grown around the recovered remains of a relay keeper. Oru can shape Aether through mineral nerves and occasionally speaks in fragments of a language the colony has never encountered.

The Reef That Remembered a City
A consumed coastal settlement reappears as a chemical memory inside a colony. Survivors recognise streets and voices in the reef’s changing forms, while the Hunger insists that this proves the city has been preserved.

The Dry Migration
A pressure-spitter colony becomes stranded on a desert world. Its effort to reach buried water brings it into conflict with Sauridian maintenance engines guarding the same aquifer. Neither side initially understands that opening it carelessly could destroy both.

factions.history:
The factories that walked away
Kilnclaw history begins with labour colonies abandoned when their freight routes failed. The inhabitants dismantled their factories, mounted the furnaces on salvaged traction frames and followed the remaining rails toward places with fuel. Generations later, the moving foundries had become cities and their maintenance crews had become clans. The Assemblage is not a single nation. It is a temporary agreement between engines travelling in roughly the same direction, maintained by bargaining, contests and the shared knowledge that every furnace eventually needs someone else’s spare parts.

A title earned in public
A Kilnclaw chief must complete a public work before claiming command: bridge a ravine, restart a dead reactor or defeat a rival machine without destroying the salvage. Strength matters, but a strong leader who cannot keep the wheels turning soon loses followers. Smaller greenskins serve as gaugesmiths, ammunition runners and negotiators. They are often exploited, yet their control of measurements gives them leverage that outsiders miss. A chief may ignore an adviser; ignoring the only person who knows the boiler’s safe pressure is another matter.

The assembly and the argument
Clans gather at great circles of parked engines to settle routes and allocate salvage. Decisions are shouted, wagered and occasionally fought over, but a binding agreement is stamped into metal and displayed on every participating furnace. The Assemblage’s wars begin when no route satisfies its appetite for ore and fuel. Some chiefs bargain for access; others declare the inhabitants of a rich world to be obstacles invented by idle people. Kilnclaw culture contains generosity toward useful strangers and an alarming indifference toward anyone it cannot recognise as a contributor.

The sound of industry
Gun mobs fight around armoured mobile workshops. Their weapons are crude in finish but often ingenious in mechanism, designed to accept several kinds of salvaged ammunition. Ram carts open lanes for weldguard infantry; boiler brutes carry enough pressure to power both limbs and close-range guns. The Marching Kiln, a towering furnace on enormous feet, converts a kill into a surge of ammunition and momentum. Its overload attack fires an extra barrage but damages its own hull. Patient opponents can bait the chief into burning through the engine before its assault reaches their line.

Rivals in the same green
Cinderjaw Freeholds view the Assemblage as noisy upstarts who have mistaken machinery for courage. Kilnclaw chiefs call the Freeholds landlords with axes. Their shared ancestry does not prevent bitter conflicts over salvage routes, and their battlefield habits differ: Freehold warbands emphasise massed charges, while Assemblage armies drag heavy industry into the firing line. Vault engineers despise their tolerances but sometimes secretly purchase Kilnclaw solutions to problems too irregular for a formal specification.

When the furnaces go quiet
The first sign of the Quiet Dread in Assemblage territory was a row of furnaces that continued to burn without making a sound. Workers could feel the pistons but could no longer hear their own tools. The affected engines were abandoned after their pressure gauges began rising with no increase in fuel. Some chiefs believe these silent furnaces offer limitless power; others insist that a machine which cannot be heard cannot be trusted. Both factions are now sending armed expeditions toward the source.

The Nine-Boiler Road
A moving city whose districts are connected by retractable bridges. Its route is voted on whenever the leading engine exhausts its fuel. Residents identify their homes by the boiler that currently supplies them rather than a fixed address.

Rivetwake
A scrapyard moon surrounded by a cloud of salvage platforms. Its clans have built an entire economy around identifying which apparently useless components still contain something another machine needs.

The Quiet Furnaces
An abandoned industrial belt where engines continue working without producing sound. Some clans treat it as a source of limitless power; others leave warning plates stating that the pressure cannot be measured honestly.

The Nine-Boiler Compact
Foreman Brakka’s coalition of mobile foundries. Its members supply disciplined gun mobs and unusually reliable heavy vehicles because their authority depends on meeting shared maintenance promises.

The Rivetmaw Routebreakers
Fast assault crews who win access to new salvage grounds by breaching obstacles in public. Their machines carry redundant rams so that a failed first impact does not require a humiliating retreat.

The Sootglass Gauge
Small technicians and Aether readers whose measurements keep the great engines alive. They rarely claim formal command but can halt an army by refusing to certify its pressure.

High Foreman Brakka Nine-Boilers
Elected after carrying a city over a salt plain on nine mismatched engines. Brakka rewards initiative and treats ammunition schedules as sacred promises. His gun mobs advance behind a moving wall of spare armour.

Ram-Queen Uzza Rivetmaw
A celebrated bridge breaker who wins route disputes through spectacular charges. Uzza measures authority by what a leader risks personally and insists that her command platform be the first machine across a contested crossing.

Gauge-Sage Tikk Sootglass
A small, meticulous pressure reader whose predictions resemble magic closely enough to unsettle his patrons. Tikk channels volatile Aether through copper gauges, correcting disasters one fraction of a second before they occur.

The Bridge With Two Owners
A Vault contract and a Kilnclaw stamped agreement both claim the same abandoned transit bridge. Each side can prove its own document authentic. Their armies arrive before either has discovered that the bridge’s supports are moving.

The Silent Shift
An entire work crew returns from the Quiet Furnaces with perfect production records and no memory of the shift. Tikk Sootglass insists the records describe an engine that has not yet been built. Rival chiefs race to assemble it before the warning can be understood.

units.name: Glassfin Skirmishers

units.name: Sun-Regent Xalatek

units.name: Crest-Marshal Issara Venn

units.rule: Charge up to Move +1 and strike for 2 AP; survivors retaliate.

units.name: Star-Reader Oq-Telan

units.rule: Caster: Aether Lance, Dread Pulse and Aegis Ward.

units.name: Dawnshield Sisters

units.name: Vigilant Sword-Sisters

units.name: Lantern Vigil Sisters

units.name: Halo Bastion Sisters

units.name: Aurora Lancers

units.name: Sanctuary Engine

units.name: Dawn Choir Battery

units.name: Sister-Artificers
units.lore: Women engineers maintain armour, hospitals and the mundane infrastructure miracles cannot replace.

units.name: Purifying Flame Sisters

units.rule: Control 2 · 100% base accuracy. Ignores cover.

units.name: High Matriarch Elyra Solenne
units.lore: A former battlefield surgeon who places the protection of strangers above the prestige of her order.
units.rule: Caster with Benediction: heal a living ally for 6 HP at 3 Aether.

units.name: Marshal Serene Valecourt
units.lore: A sister-general whose refusal to abandon prisoners once cost her an easy victory.

units.name: Saint-Errant Iona Vey

units.rule: Caster with Benediction: heal a living ally for 6 HP at 3 Aether.

units.name: Hollow-Vow Sisters

units.name: Daughters of the Thorned Halo
units.lore: Armoured women duel enemy champions to demonstrate that sacred promises can be owned.

units.name: Veil Confessors

units.name: Black Reliquary Sisters

units.name: Mourningstar Cavaliers
units.lore: Women riders command demonic steeds shaped by the ambitions of the rider, not borrowed male warlords.

units.name: Cathedral of Want

units.lore: Sister-gunners release echoes trapped inside shell casings to unmake enemy discipline.

units.name: Covenant Fleshsmiths
units.lore: Women artificers repair daemon engines by rewriting the terms of their imprisonment.

units.name: Censer-Wrath Sisters
units.lore: Armoured women spread corrosive, hallucinatory smoke around the Convent’s advancing icons.

units.name: Abbess-Maledict Vaelora Nox
units.lore: The Convent’s founder calls compassion an unfinished form of ownership and means to prove it.
units.rule: Caster with Soulfire: deal 7 damage and heal up to 5 HP at 3 Aether.

units.name: War-Prioress Sabeth Vane
units.lore: A woman general who values disciplined conquest above the ecstatic waste of her rival priestesses.
units.rule: Order an ally within 4: +15 accuracy and +1 control.

units.name: Morwenna, the Unsainted
units.lore: A formerly mortal woman transformed into the Convent’s first sovereign daemon-saint.
units.rule: Caster with Soulfire: deal 7 damage and heal up to 5 HP at 3 Aether.

units.name: Lantern Hussars
units.lore: Light cavalry on bioengineered coursers screen the rifle columns and harass enemy guns.
units.rule: Charge up to Move +1 and strike for 2 AP; survivors retaliate.

units.name: Cuirassier Exolancers
units.lore: Heavy cavalry in powered saddles delivers the decisive countercharge after the rifles fix the enemy.
units.rule: Charge up to Move +1 and strike for 2 AP; survivors retaliate.

units.name: First Marshal Cassian Rook
units.lore: A veteran of the failed crown wars, elected to hold the alliance together without becoming its emperor.
units.rule: Order an ally within 4: +15 accuracy and +1 control.

units.name: General Maerin Holt
units.lore: A former railway surveyor who wins by putting food, shells and bridges where an enemy expects exhaustion.
units.rule: Repair a friendly vehicle within 3: 7 HP, or 11 using Salvage.

units.name: Warden-General Selka Marr
units.lore: A battle scholar who treats magic as public infrastructure and refuses secret military ownership of it.
units.rule: Caster: Aether Lance, Dread Pulse and Aegis Ward.

units.name: Witness Cohort
units.lore: Witness Cohorts form the expedition’s durable centre. Every squad includes a trained advocate and emergency medic, making the formation useful after the shooting stops. Their carefully paced coil fire rewards a stationary line protected by a commander.
units.rule: Testament: nearby commanders steady armour (+1). Stationary firearm attacks gain 10 accuracy.

units.name: Breach Cadre
units.lore: Breach Cadres carry short accelerators and powered cutting tools originally built to open collapsed habitats. They are sent where a rescue route becomes a fortified kill zone, accepting expensive close-range losses to make the opening others need.
units.rule: Testament: nearby commanders steady armour (+1). Stationary firearm attacks gain 10 accuracy.

units.name: Quietus Scouts
units.lore: Quietus Scouts map structural weaknesses and enemy fields of fire. Their quiet equipment records every shot and order. In battle they trade heavy armour for range, stealth and the ability to contest a relay before the main formation arrives.
units.rule: Testament: nearby commanders steady armour (+1). Stationary firearm attacks gain 10 accuracy.

units.name: Covenant Bulwarks
units.lore: Covenant Bulwarks advance behind pressure shields mounted directly to their load frames. They are slow, costly and difficult to dislodge. Their first responsibility is to keep a safe approach open for less protected personnel.
units.rule: Testament: nearby commanders steady armour (+1). Stationary firearm attacks gain 10 accuracy.

units.name: Copperwing Lancers
units.lore: Copperwing Lancers ride compact powered outriders rather than winged creatures. Their name recalls an evacuation flight that crossed a storm using a damaged copper antenna as its final control surface. They concentrate mobility into a decisive charge.
units.rule: Testament: nearby commanders steady armour (+1). Stationary firearm attacks gain 10 accuracy.

units.name: Rescue Exoframes
units.lore: Rescue Exoframes were designed to lift collapsed reactor walls. Military versions add protected joints and heavy close-combat manipulators. Their operators still carry civilian rescue certification and frequently find their most difficult orders come after a victory.
units.rule: Testament: nearby commanders steady armour (+1). Stationary firearm attacks gain 10 accuracy.

units.name: Palladium Carrier
units.lore: Palladium Carriers transport the equipment that lets an expedition remain independent of local government. The playable formation represents their armed escort section, using a long-range cannon to remove threats to the evacuation line.
units.rule: Testament: nearby commanders steady armour (+1). Stationary firearm attacks gain 10 accuracy.

units.name: Long Vigil Battery
units.lore: Long Vigil Batteries fire calculated siege projectiles from anchored platforms. Every indirect strike requires a targeting record. Their crews are trained to withhold a technically valid shot when allied formations remain inside the predicted blast.
units.rule: Testament: nearby commanders steady armour (+1). Stationary firearm attacks gain 10 accuracy.

units.name: Corridor Burners
units.lore: Corridor Burners clear close approaches with controlled electrical discharges. Their weapons ignore conventional cover at short range. Their white armour bears black measurement marks used to judge safe distances inside smoke-filled structures.
units.rule: Testament: nearby commanders steady armour (+1). Stationary firearm attacks gain 10 accuracy.

units.name: Testament Choirwright
units.lore: Testament Choirwrights tune Aether to the resonant shapes of matter. The same discipline can shield an ally, arrest a collapsing wall or strike through armour. Their power depends on the expedition’s shared Aether reserve.
units.rule: Testament: nearby commanders steady armour (+1). Stationary firearm attacks gain 10 accuracy.

units.name: Field Restorer
units.lore: Field Restorers work under fire to keep armoured engines functioning. They mark each repair with the identity of the person who performed it, preserving accountability across centuries of reused equipment. Salvage lets their battlefield repairs restore more damage.
units.rule: Testament: nearby commanders steady armour (+1). Stationary firearm attacks gain 10 accuracy.

units.name: First Listener Cael Orison
units.lore: A veteran rescue pilot elected after refusing a ceremonial triumph. Orison links widely separated units through careful fire discipline. He worries that his reputation for restraint now prevents subordinates from reporting situations that require violence.
units.rule: Testament: nearby commanders steady armour (+1). Stationary firearm attacks gain 10 accuracy.

units.name: Breach-Marshal Iona Vey
units.lore: An engineer who survived the collapse of a station she had certified safe. Vey leads from the breach, retaining every failed structural calculation as a lesson rather than destroying the evidence. Her assault cadre treats speed as a means of rescue, never an end in itself.
units.rule: Testament: nearby commanders steady armour (+1). Stationary firearm attacks gain 10 accuracy.

units.name: Choirwright Sen Aravel
units.lore: A former acoustic archivist able to hear the deformation of metal through Aether. Aravel believes the silent relay signals are altered testimony and insists on preserving them, despite pressure from officers who would destroy the transmitters.
units.rule: Testament: nearby commanders steady armour (+1). Stationary firearm attacks gain 10 accuracy.

units.name: Lienbound Veterans
units.lore: Lienbound Veterans retain the professionalism of their rescue-legion ancestors. Their rounds carry clauses that injure the firer as they strike the target. A successful kill restores vitality, making forward aggression both doctrine and dependence.
units.rule: Blood contract: kills heal 4 HP. Attacks gain +2 damage but take 1 backlash damage.

units.name: Red Executors
units.lore: Red Executors cut open armoured shelters and drag their defenders into the open. They consider a close-range victory proof that the defeated deserved their debts. Their enhanced bodies can sustain this brutal approach longer than ordinary infantry.
units.rule: Blood contract: kills heal 4 HP. Attacks gain +2 damage but take 1 backlash damage.

units.name: Default Hunters
units.lore: Default Hunters track people who have disappeared from a ledger. Their stealth systems conceal both heat and identifying signals. In battle they seek wounded formations whose destruction will cheaply satisfy a more dangerous unit’s hunger.
units.rule: Blood contract: kills heal 4 HP. Attacks gain +2 damage but take 1 backlash damage.

units.name: Debtplate Wardens
units.lore: Debtplate Wardens wear armour inscribed with the obligations of entire districts. The plates can survive immense punishment, but every replacement creates another claim against the population. Their resilience is built from a system that cannot permit peace.
units.rule: Blood contract: kills heal 4 HP. Attacks gain +2 damage but take 1 backlash damage.

units.name: Vow-Riders
units.lore: Vow-Riders pilot narrow bound outriders chained to their armour. A rider who falls remains attached to the machine until the next battle is won. Their charges combine veteran discipline with the urgency of avoiding that fate.
units.rule: Blood contract: kills heal 4 HP. Attacks gain +2 damage but take 1 backlash damage.

units.name: Bound Penitents
units.lore: Bound Penitents are augmented survivors whose bodies have been converted into collateral. Their immense manipulators were once rescue tools. They now break the same kinds of shelters their ancestors opened to save people.
units.rule: Blood contract: kills heal 4 HP. Attacks gain +2 damage but take 1 backlash damage.

units.name: Iron Indenture
units.lore: Iron Indentures carry a family’s confiscated industrial engine inside a tank hull. The cannon’s recoil is absorbed by the binding mechanism. Disabling the vehicle can release its prisoners, but a careless explosion destroys them with it.
units.rule: Blood contract: kills heal 4 HP. Attacks gain +2 damage but take 1 backlash damage.

units.name: Ledger Bombard
units.lore: Ledger Bombards launch sealed contract fragments inside siege charges. The supernatural language is symbolic in this tactical version: the formation uses the same bracing, minimum-range and friendly-fire constraints as other indirect artillery.
units.rule: Blood contract: kills heal 4 HP. Attacks gain +2 damage but take 1 backlash damage.

units.name: Covenant Scorchers
units.lore: Covenant Scorchers burn passages through both cover and evidence. Their crews are deployed when command wants a settlement taken without leaving intact records of the collection. Short reach makes them vulnerable before they close.
units.rule: Blood contract: kills heal 4 HP. Attacks gain +2 damage but take 1 backlash damage.

units.name: Null Notaries
units.lore: Null Notaries turn names and promises into Aether patterns. A formation may fight for hours without noticing that its command acknowledgements have become part of an enemy ritual. Their tactical spells still draw from a finite shared reserve.
units.rule: Blood contract: kills heal 4 HP. Attacks gain +2 damage but take 1 backlash damage.

units.name: Chainwrights
units.lore: Chainwrights maintain the interfaces between machinery and bound consciousness. They speak soothingly to engines they are unwilling to free. Their repair crews recover salvage with the same efficiency they use to recover defaulting debtors.
units.rule: Blood contract: kills heal 4 HP. Attacks gain +2 damage but take 1 backlash damage.

units.name: Executor Mael Rusk
units.lore: The last surviving officer to sign the corridor bargain. Rusk remembers the exact number of people saved and cannot bear to admit that his effort to honour them has become a greater disaster. His orders drive relentless close-range fire.
units.rule: Blood contract: kills heal 4 HP. Attacks gain +2 damage but take 1 backlash damage.

units.name: Lady Nerezza Vow-Eater
units.lore: A duellist who purchased her first command by taking the debts of an entire city. Each victory adds another name to her armour. She regards compassion as a weakness in the wording of a contract and seeks opponents whose defeat will prove it.
units.rule: Blood contract: kills heal 4 HP. Attacks gain +2 damage but take 1 backlash damage.

units.name: Notary Ossian Null
units.lore: A sorcerer whose body was erased from every official register. Null speaks through a mask suspended above an empty pressure suit and uses stolen signatures to turn battlefield casualties into regenerative power.
units.rule: Blood contract: kills heal 4 HP. Attacks gain +2 damage but take 1 backlash damage.

units.name: Needle Shoal
units.lore: Needle Shoals are numerous small organisms whose shared colour signals coordinate bursts of mineral darts. They screen more valuable organs and occupy relay sites. Their apparent uniformity conceals inherited memories that diverge with every feeding.
units.rule: Assimilation: kills restore 3 HP. Creatures near a commander gain +1 damage and resist suppression.

units.name: Harrower Brood
units.lore: Harrower Broods grow dense forelimbs around sacrificial cutting edges. A damaged blade is shed and regrown from stored minerals. They are the colony’s answer to resistant prey that ordinary needle fire cannot safely approach.
units.rule: Assimilation: kills restore 3 HP. Creatures near a commander gain +1 damage and resist suppression.

units.name: Echo Skimmers
units.lore: Echo Skimmers sense movement through pressure changes and electromagnetic disturbances. Their light bodies cross difficult approaches quickly. They relay impressions to nearby knots, allowing the colony to investigate before committing its heaviest organisms.
units.rule: Assimilation: kills restore 3 HP. Creatures near a commander gain +1 damage and resist suppression.

units.name: Reefguard Cysts
units.lore: Reefguard Cysts concentrate shell material around vulnerable neural tissue. Their slow movement reflects the cost of carrying that protection. They hold positions long enough for more flexible organisms to adapt the surrounding environment.
units.rule: Assimilation: kills restore 3 HP. Creatures near a commander gain +1 damage and resist suppression.

units.name: Sickle Swimmers
units.lore: Sickle Swimmers move on muscular wave-like limbs, carrying hooks originally used to anchor themselves in turbulent currents. On land those hooks turn a rapid approach into a violent charge. Their name preserves the ocean in their inherited memory.
units.rule: Assimilation: kills restore 3 HP. Creatures near a commander gain +1 damage and resist suppression.

units.name: Breakwater Brutes
units.lore: Breakwater Brutes evolved to crack the mineral shells of rival colonial organisms. Their immense limbs serve the same purpose against armoured vehicles. They lack the long-range precision of specialised gun organisms and depend on screening shoals.
units.rule: Assimilation: kills restore 3 HP. Creatures near a commander gain +1 damage and resist suppression.

units.name: Shellback Carrier
units.lore: Shellback Carriers enclose a compressed fluid chamber inside layered armour. Their cannon vents that chamber through a directional organ. The living hull is resilient, but its specialised internal pressure makes it a poor close-combat predator.
units.rule: Assimilation: kills restore 3 HP. Creatures near a commander gain +1 damage and resist suppression.

units.name: Pressure-Spitter
units.lore: Pressure-Spitters root themselves before launching living corrosive pods in high arcs. Their rooted firing stance becomes the artillery bracing rule. The pods cannot distinguish friend from foe when they rupture, preserving the tactical danger of friendly fire.
units.rule: Assimilation: kills restore 3 HP. Creatures near a commander gain +1 damage and resist suppression.

units.name: Caustic Shoal
units.lore: Caustic Shoals expel reactive fluids that flow around ordinary cover. Their fragile spray organs require them to approach close to the target. The colony uses them to clear entrenched prey after other organisms have drawn its attention.
units.rule: Assimilation: kills restore 3 HP. Creatures near a commander gain +1 damage and resist suppression.

units.name: Memory Lattice
units.lore: Memory Lattices retain enough inherited experience to shape Aether deliberately. Their mineral nerves act as resonators. They can coordinate a local colony and strike through armour, but remain dependent on the same scarce energy that sustains other powers’ magic.
units.rule: Assimilation: kills restore 3 HP. Creatures near a commander gain +1 damage and resist suppression.

units.name: Mender Polyps
units.lore: Mender Polyps dissolve damaged armour and rebuild it into usable structures. In the tactical adaptation their repair ability services allied armoured organisms. Salvage represents minerals and viable tissue recovered from the battlefield.
units.rule: Assimilation: kills restore 3 HP. Creatures near a commander gain +1 damage and resist suppression.

units.name: First Current Sere
units.lore: A consensus knot carrying the memory of the first successful journey through vacuum. Sere advances cautiously, using cheap bodies to measure threats before committing the colony’s irreplaceable organs.
units.rule: Assimilation: kills restore 3 HP. Creatures near a commander gain +1 damage and resist suppression.

units.name: The Ninth Appetite
units.lore: A predator whose successive bodies have each survived starvation. It favours violent concentration, breaking a single line before spreading through the breach. Its memories increasingly equate resistance with nourishment.
units.rule: Assimilation: kills restore 3 HP. Creatures near a commander gain +1 damage and resist suppression.

units.name: Lattice-Mother Oru
units.lore: A symbiotic intelligence grown around the recovered remains of a relay keeper. Oru can shape Aether through mineral nerves and occasionally speaks in fragments of a language the colony has never encountered.
units.rule: Assimilation: kills restore 3 HP. Creatures near a commander gain +1 damage and resist suppression.

units.name: Rivet Gunmob
units.lore: Rivet Gunmobs carry robust weapons adapted from industrial fastener launchers. They are less accurate than elite human files but compensate with tough bodies and forceful fire. Chiefs keep them close enough to receive both orders and replacement plates.
units.rule: Boiler rush: moved attacks gain +3 melee damage; each kill adds an extra Aether. Armour is strongest around commanders.

units.name: Weldguard Mob
units.lore: Weldguard Mobs protect working engineers in the middle of an assault. Their heavy guns are paired with tools capable of cutting seized machinery free. They judge a victory partly by how much usable equipment remains afterwards.
units.rule: Boiler rush: moved attacks gain +3 melee damage; each kill adds an extra Aether. Armour is strongest around commanders.

units.name: Soot Runners
units.lore: Soot Runners scout routes and inspect salvage before the foundries commit to a march. Their lightly protected teams prefer useful information to a fair fight. The longest-range guns are often assembled from several incompatible but carefully measured parts.
units.rule: Boiler rush: moved attacks gain +3 melee damage; each kill adds an extra Aether. Armour is strongest around commanders.

units.name: Boilerplate Guard
units.lore: Boilerplate Guards wear overlapping sections of retired pressure vessels. The armour is heavy, hot and remarkably resilient. Their job is to remain in the breach while crews behind them convert captured territory into a working route.
units.rule: Boiler rush: moved attacks gain +3 melee damage; each kill adds an extra Aether. Armour is strongest around commanders.

units.name: Ram Carts
units.lore: Ram Carts are compact racing engines with reinforced fronts and almost no concern for comfort. Their crews approach combat as a public test of workmanship. A successful charge advertises the chief who funded the machine.
units.rule: Boiler rush: moved attacks gain +3 melee damage; each kill adds an extra Aether. Armour is strongest around commanders.

units.name: Piston Brutes
units.lore: Piston Brutes strap industrial actuators to already powerful bodies. The resulting strength can tear open armour, provided the gaugesmith has kept every joint supplied with pressure. They are feared in melee and dependent on a functioning supply line.
units.rule: Boiler rush: moved attacks gain +3 melee damage; each kill adds an extra Aether. Armour is strongest around commanders.

units.name: Scrap Hauler
units.lore: Scrap Haulers combine cargo capacity with a large turret gun. The military formation represents the armed machines at the head of a foundry convoy. Their armour protects valuable tools as much as the crew.
units.rule: Boiler rush: moved attacks gain +3 melee damage; each kill adds an extra Aether. Armour is strongest around commanders.

units.name: Furnace Lobber
units.lore: Furnace Lobbers fire heavy charges made from whatever the clan can safely seal inside a shell. Their trajectories remain predictable enough to require proper deployment and minimum range. Nearby allies are not protected from the resulting blast.
units.rule: Boiler rush: moved attacks gain +3 melee damage; each kill adds an extra Aether. Armour is strongest around commanders.

units.name: Slag Throwers
units.lore: Slag Throwers use industrial waste as short-range ammunition. The material floods trenches and exposed firing positions, defeating cover rather than armour at a distance. Their crews must advance under protection to make the weapon useful.
units.rule: Boiler rush: moved attacks gain +3 melee damage; each kill adds an extra Aether. Armour is strongest around commanders.

units.name: Gauge Sages
units.lore: Gauge Sages read physical pressure and Aether resonance through the same collection of instruments. Their apparent improvisation depends on years of careful measurement. A spectacular spell is usually preceded by a very quiet correction to a valve.
units.rule: Boiler rush: moved attacks gain +3 melee damage; each kill adds an extra Aether. Armour is strongest around commanders.

units.name: Patch Crews
units.lore: Patch Crews keep the Assemblage’s mismatched vehicles moving. Their pride lies in making a repair with whatever the previous owner left behind. Salvage improves their battlefield repairs, rewarding armies that keep engineers close to damaged engines.
units.rule: Boiler rush: moved attacks gain +3 melee damage; each kill adds an extra Aether. Armour is strongest around commanders.

units.name: High Foreman Brakka Nine-Boilers
units.lore: Elected after carrying a city over a salt plain on nine mismatched engines. Brakka rewards initiative and treats ammunition schedules as sacred promises. His gun mobs advance behind a moving wall of spare armour.
units.rule: Boiler rush: moved attacks gain +3 melee damage; each kill adds an extra Aether. Armour is strongest around commanders.

units.name: Ram-Queen Uzza Rivetmaw
units.lore: A celebrated bridge breaker who wins route disputes through spectacular charges. Uzza measures authority by what a leader risks personally and insists that her command platform be the first machine across a contested crossing.
units.rule: Boiler rush: moved attacks gain +3 melee damage; each kill adds an extra Aether. Armour is strongest around commanders.

units.name: Gauge-Sage Tikk Sootglass
units.lore: A small, meticulous pressure reader whose predictions resemble magic closely enough to unsettle his patrons. Tikk channels volatile Aether through copper gauges, correcting disasters one fraction of a second before they occur.
units.rule: Boiler rush: moved attacks gain +3 melee damage; each kill adds an extra Aether. Armour is strongest around commanders.

units.name: Verminia, the Walking Womb-Palace
units.rule: Birth a Clawrat formation every turn at no Aether cost, provided an adjacent cell and active brood slot are free. Destroyed broods free slots.
units.lore: Verminia the All-Mother is codex-derived (pp.14–15,89). Her walking battlefield manifestation, titan statistics and renewable brood rules are original game adaptations requested by the user.

units.name: Concord Atlas
units.rule: Raise a 6-point shield on every ally within 4.
units.lore: An original titan of the Aurelian Compact. Raise a 6-point shield on every ally within 4. Its silhouette and strategic role reflect the faction’s institutions rather than a shared reskinned chassis.

units.name: Worldbreaker Gromm
units.rule: Stomp every adjacent enemy for 18 damage and 2 suppression.
units.lore: An original titan of the Cinderjaw Freeholds. Stomp every adjacent enemy for 18 damage and 2 suppression. Its silhouette and strategic role reflect the faction’s institutions rather than a shared reskinned chassis.

units.name: Graven Mountain Siege Engine
units.rule: Brace, then fire a 48-damage regiment-breaker: 55% base accuracy, blast radius 1. Movement breaks the brace.
units.lore: An original titan of the Kharad Vault Concord. Brace, then fire a 48-damage regiment-breaker: 55% base accuracy, blast radius 1. Movement breaks the brace. Its silhouette and strategic role reflect the faction’s institutions rather than a shared reskinned chassis.

units.name: Astral Crown Seraph
units.rule: A piercing beam deals 16 damage to all enemies in the selected row.
units.lore: An original titan of the Lumen Arc Principalities. A piercing beam deals 16 damage to all enemies in the selected row. Its silhouette and strategic role reflect the faction’s institutions rather than a shared reskinned chassis.

units.name: Nightglass Leviathan
units.rule: Slip up to 6 cells and shroud allies within 3, reducing incoming accuracy.

setting:
The Crown was a network of orbital engines, buried relays and resonant roads that allowed many peoples to share energy between worlds. Its makers are unknown. Successive empires claimed to have built it; surviving maintenance inscriptions contradict all of them. When the Crown fractured, its currents escaped into the material universe as Aether. Machines continued to work, but now a correctly shaped promise, a disciplined mind or a remembered name could sometimes change what the machine did.

The present wars are fought over the surviving relays. A relay can heat a city, stabilise a starship passage, sustain an ancestor archive or keep a hungry dimension closed. Armies therefore contest infrastructure as fiercely as territory. Guns remain reliable, artillery breaks fixed positions, and armour keeps soldiers alive. Magic supplies advantages that machinery cannot reproduce, but depends on trained practitioners and scarce coherent Aether. None of these tools makes the others obsolete.

The Ash Calendar begins with the first measured failure of the Crown. The current setting year is 312 AC. These dates are original The Quiet Dread chronology, not dates in the Verminhorde source. The Dominion enters this setting through the deep relay routes; its provided history remains a separate source tradition. References here to its relations with new factions are explicitly new crossover-setting material.

There is no single moral explanation for the war. The Compact seeks survivable government, the Vaults defend contracts, the Synod protects living worlds and the Continuum protects identity beyond death. Some factions can negotiate. Others make negotiation a weapon. The Daughters of the Unbroken Dawn practise sincere, demanding goodness; the Hollow Star deliberately subordinates other lives to power. Their conflict is not proof that all faith is fraud. It is a conflict over what faith permits its wielders to do.

The Quiet Dread names the silence spreading behind apparently functioning relays. Four new powers follow that silence into the contested worlds.
